#### Q73: How does the Iterator Pattern decouple algorithms from data structures?
**Companies**: Google (Graph Traversals), Amazon (Pagination), Java Collections, Python Iterators
**Difficulty**: **Medium** (Behavioral Pattern / Traversal)
**Category**: Behavioral Patterns, Algorithms

---

### **1. Conceptual Overview & Motivation**

**The "Why": Decoupling Traversal from Storage**
Imagine a **Social Network**. Internally, it might store users in a:
*   `List<User>` (Simple)
*   `HashMap<String, User>` (Fast Lookup)
*   `AdjacencyMatrix` (Dense Graph)
*   `Neo4j Driver` (Graph DB)

**The Problem**: If you expose the internal structure (`List<User> list = network.getUsers()`), you **leak implementation details**. If you switch to a Graph DB later, *every single client* iterating over users breaks.

**The Solution**: The **Iterator Pattern**.
The Container provides a uniform interface (`next()`, `hasNext()`) to traverse elements. The Client effectively says: *"I don't care how you store data, just give me the next one."*

**Real-World Analogies**:
1.  **Spotify Shuffle**: You hit "Next Song". You don't know the exact index, random seed, or database query used to pick it. You just get an audio stream.
2.  **TV Remote**: Channel UP. You don't know the frequency map.
3.  **Database Cursor**: `ResultSet.next()` fetches rows one by one, managing network buffers and disk I/O behind the scenes.

---

### **2. Visualization: Internal Pointer Mechanics**

<div id="iterator-viz" style="border: 1px solid #ccc; padding: 20px; border-radius: 8px; background: #1e1e1e; color: #fff;">
    <svg id="iter-svg" width="800" height="250"></svg>
    <div style="margin-top: 15px; display: flex; gap: 10px;">
        <button onclick="iterNext()" style="padding: 8px; background: #4caf50; border: none; color: white; border-radius: 4px; cursor: pointer;">it.next()</button>
        <button onclick="iterReset()" style="padding: 8px; background: #ff9800; border: none; color: white; border-radius: 4px; cursor: pointer;">Reset</button>
        <select id="struct-select" onchange="changeStruct()" style="padding: 8px; border-radius: 4px;">
            <option value="array">ArrayList (Index)</option>
            <option value="linked">LinkedList (Node Ptr)</option>
            <option value="tree">Tree (DFS Stack)</option>
        </select>
    </div>
    <div id="iter-log" style="margin-top: 10px; font-family: monospace; font-size: 14px; color: #aaa;">Status: Ready</div>
</div>

<script src="https://d3js.org/d3.v7.min.js"></script>
<script>
    const iterSvg = d3.select("#iter-svg");
    let currentIndex = -1;
    let structureType = "array";
    
    // Data Models
    const arrayData = [10, 20, 30, 40, 50];
    const linkedData = [
        {id: "Head", x: 50, val: 10}, 
        {id: "N2", x: 200, val: 20}, 
        {id: "N3", x: 350, val: 30}, 
        {id: "Tail", x: 500, val: 40}
    ];
    
    // Tree Nodes: A (B (D, E), C (F))
    const treeData = {
        name: "A", 
        children: [
            { name: "B", children: [{name: "D"}, {name: "E"}] },
            { name: "C", children: [{name: "F"}] }
        ]
    };
    
    // DFS Order for Tree
    const treeOrder = ["A", "B", "D", "E", "C", "F"];

    function draw() {
        iterSvg.selectAll("*").remove();
        currentIndex = -1;
        document.getElementById("iter-log").innerText = "Status: Iterator Created";

        if (structureType === "array") drawArray();
        else if (structureType === "linked") drawLinked();
        else if (structureType === "tree") drawTree();
    }

    function drawArray() {
        iterSvg.selectAll("rect")
            .data(arrayData)
            .enter().append("rect")
            .attr("x", (d,i) => 50 + i*100)
            .attr("y", 100)
            .attr("width", 80)
            .attr("height", 50)
            .attr("fill", "#333")
            .attr("stroke", "#fff");

        iterSvg.selectAll("text")
            .data(arrayData)
            .enter().append("text")
            .attr("x", (d,i) => 90 + i*100)
            .attr("y", 130)
            .attr("text-anchor", "middle")
            .attr("fill", "#fff")
            .text(d => d);
            
        // Iterator Pointer
        iterSvg.append("path")
            .attr("id", "pointer")
            .attr("d", "M 90 160 L 80 180 L 100 180 Z")
            .attr("fill", "#00bcd4")
            .attr("transform", "translate(-100,0)"); // Hidden initially
    }

    function drawLinked() {
        // Nodes
        iterSvg.selectAll("circle")
            .data(linkedData)
            .enter().append("circle")
            .attr("cx", d => d.x)
            .attr("cy", 125)
            .attr("r", 30)
            .attr("fill", "#333")
            .attr("stroke", "#fff");
            
        // Links
        iterSvg.selectAll("line")
            .data(linkedData.slice(0, -1))
            .enter().append("line")
            .attr("x1", d => d.x + 30)
            .attr("y1", 125)
            .attr("x2", (d,i) => linkedData[i+1].x - 30)
            .attr("y2", 125)
            .attr("stroke", "#fff")
            .attr("marker-end", "url(#arrow)");
            
        iterSvg.selectAll("text")
            .data(linkedData)
            .enter().append("text")
            .attr("x", d => d.x)
            .attr("y", 130)
            .attr("text-anchor", "middle")
            .attr("fill", "#fff")
            .text(d => d.val);
            
        // Arrow Marker
        iterSvg.append("defs").append("marker")
            .attr("id", "arrow")
            .attr("viewBox", "0 0 10 10")
            .attr("refX", 10)
            .attr("refY", 5)
            .attr("markerWidth", 6)
            .attr("markerHeight", 6)
            .attr("orient", "auto")
            .append("path")
            .attr("d", "M 0 0 L 10 5 L 0 10 z")
            .attr("fill", "#fff");
            
        // Pointer
        iterSvg.append("circle")
            .attr("id", "pointer")
            .attr("r", 10)
            .attr("fill", "#00bcd4")
            .attr("cx", -50) // Hidden
            .attr("cy", 125);
    }

    function drawTree() {
       const root = d3.hierarchy(treeData);
       const treeLayout = d3.tree().size([700, 200]);
       treeLayout(root);
       
       iterSvg.selectAll('line')
            .data(root.links())
            .enter().append('line')
            .attr('x1', d => d.source.x + 50)
            .attr('y1', d => d.source.y + 30)
            .attr('x2', d => d.target.x + 50)
            .attr('y2', d => d.target.y + 30)
            .attr('stroke', '#fff');

       const nodes = iterSvg.selectAll('circle')
            .data(root.descendants())
            .enter().append('g')
            .attr('transform', d => `translate(${d.x + 50},${d.y + 30})`);
            
       nodes.append('circle').attr('r', 20).attr('fill', '#333').attr('stroke', '#fff');
       nodes.append('text').text(d => d.data.name).attr('dy', 5).attr('text-anchor', 'middle').attr('fill', '#fff');
       
       // Map names to coordinates for pointer
       window.treeCoords = {};
       root.descendants().forEach(d => {
           window.treeCoords[d.data.name] = {x: d.x + 50, y: d.y + 30};
       });
       
       iterSvg.append("circle")
            .attr("id", "pointer")
            .attr("r", 5)
            .attr("fill", "#00bcd4")
            .attr("cx", -50)
            .attr("cy", -50);
    }

    function iterNext() {
        currentIndex++;
        const log = document.getElementById("iter-log");
        
        if (structureType === "array") {
            if (currentIndex >= arrayData.length) {
                log.innerText = "Status: hasNext() == false";
                currentIndex = arrayData.length;
                return;
            }
            d3.select("#pointer")
                .transition()
                .duration(500)
                .attr("transform", `translate(${currentIndex * 100}, 0)`);
            log.innerText = `Status: Returned ${arrayData[currentIndex]}, Index -> ${currentIndex + 1}`;
        }
        else if (structureType === "linked") {
            if (currentIndex >= linkedData.length) {
                log.innerText = "Status: hasNext() == false";
                return;
            }
            d3.select("#pointer")
                .transition()
                .duration(500)
                .attr("cx", linkedData[currentIndex].x);
            log.innerText = `Status: Current Node -> ${linkedData[currentIndex].val}`;
        }
        else if (structureType === "tree") {
            if (currentIndex >= treeOrder.length) {
                log.innerText = "Status: hasNext() == false";
                return;
            }
            const name = treeOrder[currentIndex];
            const coords = window.treeCoords[name];
            d3.select("#pointer")
                .transition()
                .duration(500)
                .attr("cx", coords.x)
                .attr("cy", coords.y);
            log.innerText = `Status: DFS Vist -> ${name}`;
        }
    }

    function iterReset() {
        draw();
    }
    
    function changeStruct() {
        structureType = document.getElementById("struct-select").value;
        draw();
    }

    draw(); // Init
</script>

---

### **3. Comprehensive Definition**

**Formal Definition**:
> Provide a way to access the elements of an aggregate object sequentially without exposing its underlying representation.

**The Key Roles**:
1.  **Iterator**: The Interface (`hasNext()`, `next()`, `remove()`).
2.  **Concrete Iterator**: Keeps track of position (e.g., `cursor`, `index`, `currentNode`).
3.  **Iterable (Aggregate)**: The uniform interface returning an Iterator (`iterator()`).
4.  **Client**: Loops through elements without knowing if it's an Array or a Tree.

---

### **4. Project 1: Enterprise Database Pagination (Cursor vs Offset)**

In Enterprise APIs (like Stripe, Twitter, DynamoDB), you never return **all** results. You iterate pages.
We will compare two Iterators for fetching data from a mock Database.

#### 4.1. The Mock Database
```java
import java.util.*;
import java.util.concurrent.*;

// Simulated Database Row
class UserRecord {
    String id;
    long timestamp; // Sort Key
    
    public UserRecord(String id, long timestamp) {
        this.id = id;
        this.timestamp = timestamp;
    }
    
    @Override public String toString() { return "[" + id + " @ " + timestamp + "]"; }
}

// Simulated DB Table
class Database {
    private List<UserRecord> storage = new ArrayList<>();
    
    public Database() {
        // Populate 100 records sorted by timestamp
        for(int i=0; i<100; i++) {
            storage.add(new UserRecord("usr_" + i, 1000 + i));
        }
    }
    
    // METHOD 1: Offset (Simulates "LIMIT 10 OFFSET 50")
    // PROBLEM: O(Offset + Limit). Slow for deep pages.
    public List<UserRecord> queryOffset(int offset, int limit) {
        System.out.println("LOG: SELECT * FROM users OFFSET " + offset + " LIMIT " + limit);
        try { Thread.sleep(10); } catch(Exception e) {} // Sim Latency
        
        if (offset >= storage.size()) return Collections.emptyList();
        return storage.subList(offset, Math.min(offset + limit, storage.size()));
    }
    
    // METHOD 2: Cursor (Simulates "WHERE timestamp > X LIMIT 10")
    // BENEFIT: O(Limit). Fast regardless of depth.
    public List<UserRecord> queryCursor(long lastSeenTimestamp, int limit) {
        System.out.println("LOG: SELECT * FROM users WHERE ts > " + lastSeenTimestamp + " LIMIT " + limit);
        try { Thread.sleep(10); } catch(Exception e) {} 
        
        List<UserRecord> result = new ArrayList<>();
        int count = 0;
        for (UserRecord r : storage) {
            if (r.timestamp > lastSeenTimestamp) {
                result.add(r);
                count++;
                if (count == limit) break;
            }
        }
        return result;
    }
}
```

#### 4.2. Offset Iterator (The Anti-Pattern for Scale)
This iterator works like standard pagination logic (Page 1, Page 2...).

```java
class OffsetIterator implements Iterator<List<UserRecord>> {
    private Database db;
    private int currentOffset = 0;
    private int pageSize = 10;
    private List<UserRecord> nextBatch;
    
    public OffsetIterator(Database db) {
        this.db = db;
        this.nextBatch = db.queryOffset(0, pageSize); // Prefetch
    }
    
    @Override
    public boolean hasNext() {
        return !nextBatch.isEmpty();
    }
    
    @Override
    public List<UserRecord> next() {
        List<UserRecord> batch = nextBatch;
        currentOffset += pageSize;
        nextBatch = db.queryOffset(currentOffset, pageSize);
        return batch;
    }
}
```

#### 4.3. Cursor Iterator (The Enterprise Standard)
This iterator uses the **last seen item** as a pointer for the next batch. This is stateless and efficient.

```java
class CursorIterator implements Iterator<List<UserRecord>> {
    private Database db;
    private long lastTimestamp = 0; // The Cursor
    private int pageSize = 10;
    private List<UserRecord> nextBatch;
    
    public CursorIterator(Database db) {
        this.db = db;
        this.nextBatch = db.queryCursor(0, pageSize);
    }
    
    @Override
    public boolean hasNext() {
        return !nextBatch.isEmpty();
    }
    
    @Override
    public List<UserRecord> next() {
        List<UserRecord> batch = nextBatch;
        
        // Update cursor to the last item of the batch
        UserRecord lastItem = batch.get(batch.size() - 1);
        this.lastTimestamp = lastItem.timestamp;
        
        // Fetch next page starting AFTER the cursor
        nextBatch = db.queryCursor(lastTimestamp, pageSize);
        return batch;
    }
}

public class PaginationDemo {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        Database db = new Database();
        
        System.out.println("--- 1. OFFSET PAGINATION ---");
        Iterator<List<UserRecord>> offIter = new OffsetIterator(db);
        while(offIter.hasNext()) {
            System.out.println("Page: " + offIter.next().size() + " records");
        }
        
        System.out.println("\n--- 2. CURSOR PAGINATION ---");
        Iterator<List<UserRecord>> curIter = new CursorIterator(db);
        while(curIter.hasNext()) {
             System.out.println("Page: " + curIter.next().size() + " records");
        }
    }
}
```

> [!TIP]
> **Performance**: Offset pagination gets slower the deeper you go ($O(N)$). Cursor pagination remains constant time ($O(1)$) because indexes allow jumping directly to the timestamp. **Always prefer Cursors for APIs.**

### **5. Project 2: Secure File System Walker (Recursive)**

A common task: "Find all `.log` files in this directory and subdirectories."
We need a **Recursive Iterator** that flattens a Tree structure into a linear stream of files.

#### 5.1. The Component
```java
import java.io.File;
import java.util.*;

class SecureFileIterator implements Iterator<File> {
    private Stack<Iterator<File>> stack = new Stack<>();
    private File nextFile;
    private int maxDepth;
    private int currentDepth = 0;
    
    // Security: Cycle Detection for Symlinks
    private Set<String> visitedPaths = new HashSet<>();

    public SecureFileIterator(File root, int maxDepth) {
        this.maxDepth = maxDepth;
        if (root.isDirectory()) {
            stack.push(Arrays.asList(root.listFiles()).iterator());
            visitedPaths.add(root.getAbsolutePath());
        }
        advance();
    }

    private void advance() {
        nextFile = null;
        
        while (!stack.isEmpty()) {
            Iterator<File> currentIter = stack.peek();
            
            if (currentIter.hasNext()) {
                File candidate = currentIter.next();
                
                try {
                    // Security Check: Symlink Cycle
                    String path = candidate.getCanonicalPath();
                    if (visitedPaths.contains(path)) {
                        System.out.println("⚠️ CYCLE DETECTED: " + path);
                        continue; // Skip
                    }
                    
                    if (candidate.isDirectory()) {
                        if (stack.size() < maxDepth) {
                            visitedPaths.add(path);
                            // Dive Deeper (Push new iterator)
                            File[] children = candidate.listFiles();
                            if (children != null) {
                                stack.push(Arrays.asList(children).iterator());
                            }
                        } else {
                            System.out.println("⚠️ MAX DEPTH REACHED: " + candidate.getName());
                        }
                    } else {
                        // It's a file, we found our next item!
                        nextFile = candidate;
                        return;
                    }
                } catch (Exception e) {
                    // Permission Denial? Skip.
                    System.err.println("Access Denied: " + candidate.getName());
                }
            } else {
                // Current directory finished
                stack.pop();
                visitedPaths.remove(stack.size()); // Optional: cleanup visited for siblings? Usually Keep for global cycle check.
            }
        }
    }

    @Override
    public boolean hasNext() {
        return nextFile != null;
    }

    @Override
    public File next() {
        if (!hasNext()) throw new NoSuchElementException();
        File result = nextFile;
        advance(); // Premeditatively find the next one
        return result;
    }
}
```

> [!IMPORTANT]
> **Security Aspect**: **Symlink Loops** (Folder A -> Folder B -> Folder A) can cause infinite recursion and crash a server. Always assume the filesystem is hostile.

### **6. Project 3: Zero-Allocation Ring Buffer Iterator (HFT)**

In High-Frequency Trading (HFT), creating `new Iterator()` objects generates Garbage. GC pauses kill latency.
We need an Iterator that **reuses itself** or uses primitive access patterns.

#### 6.1. The Ring Buffer
A fixed-size array that overwrite old data.
`[ 10, 20, 30, 40 ]` -> Push 50 -> `[ 50, 20, 30, 40 ]`

```java
class RingBuffer<T> implements Iterable<T> {
    private T[] data;
    private int head = 0;
    private int tail = 0;
    private int size = 0;
    private int capacity;
    
    // The Reusable Iterator (Flyweight style)
    private final ReusableIterator iterator = new ReusableIterator();

    @SuppressWarnings("unchecked")
    public RingBuffer(int capacity) {
        this.capacity = capacity;
        this.data = (T[]) new Object[capacity];
    }

    public void add(T item) {
        if (size == capacity) {
            // Overwrite head (Circular)
            head = (head + 1) % capacity;
            size--; 
        }
        data[tail] = item;
        tail = (tail + 1) % capacity;
        size++;
    }

    @Override
    public Iterator<T> iterator() {
        // RESET the existing iterator instead of creating new
        iterator.reset();
        return iterator;
    }

    // Inner Class - carefully designed to stay on stack if possible (Escape Analysis)
    private class ReusableIterator implements Iterator<T> {
        private int currentCount = 0;
        private int currentIndex = 0;

        public void reset() {
            this.currentCount = 0;
            this.currentIndex = head;
        }

        @Override
        public boolean hasNext() {
            return currentCount < size;
        }

        @Override
        public T next() {
            if (!hasNext()) throw new NoSuchElementException();
            T val = data[currentIndex];
            currentIndex = (currentIndex + 1) % capacity;
            currentCount++;
            return val;
        }
    }
}

public class HFTDemo {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        RingBuffer<String> prices = new RingBuffer<>(3);
        
        prices.add("100.00");
        prices.add("100.05");
        prices.add("100.10");
        
        // Overflow
        prices.add("100.15"); // Should overwrite 100.00
        
        System.out.println("Processing Prices (Zero GC):");
        // Implicitly calls iterator()
        for (String p : prices) {
            System.out.println("Price: " + p);
        }
        
        // Re-run (Uses SAME Iterator object)
        System.out.println("\nSecond Pass:");
        for (String p : prices) {
            System.out.print(p + " ");
        }
    }
}
```

> [!TIP]
> **Memory Layout**: This design keeps the iterator hot in the CPU cache and triggers **Zero GCs** during the loop. Essential for systems requiring < 1ms latency.

### **7. Project 4: "Merge K Sorted Lists" Iterator (Distributed Logs)**

**Scenario**: You have 10 log files, each sorted by timestamp. You want to merge them into **one** chronological stream without loading all files into memory.
**Solution**: A `MergeIterator` using a `PriorityQueue` and `PeekingIterator`.

```java
import java.util.*;

// Interface that allows looking ahead without consuming
interface PeekingIterator<T> extends Iterator<T> {
    T peek();
}

class LogEntry implements Comparable<LogEntry> {
    long timestamp;
    String msg;

    public LogEntry(long t, String m) { timestamp = t; msg = m; }
    public int compareTo(LogEntry other) { return Long.compare(this.timestamp, other.timestamp); }
    public String toString() { return timestamp + ": " + msg; }
}

class SortedListIterator implements PeekingIterator<LogEntry> {
    private Iterator<LogEntry> backing;
    private LogEntry nextItem;

    public SortedListIterator(List<LogEntry> list) {
        this.backing = list.iterator();
        advance();
    }

    private void advance() {
        nextItem = backing.hasNext() ? backing.next() : null;
    }

    public boolean hasNext() { return nextItem != null; }
    public LogEntry next() {
        LogEntry res = nextItem;
        advance();
        return res;
    }
    public LogEntry peek() { return nextItem; }
}

class MergingIterator implements Iterator<LogEntry> {
    private PriorityQueue<PeekingIterator<LogEntry>> minHeap;

    public MergingIterator(List<PeekingIterator<LogEntry>> iterators) {
        // Min-Heap orders iterators by their CURRENT (peeked) element
        minHeap = new PriorityQueue<>((a, b) -> a.peek().compareTo(b.peek()));
        
        for (PeekingIterator<LogEntry> it : iterators) {
            if (it.hasNext()) minHeap.add(it);
        }
    }

    public boolean hasNext() { return !minHeap.isEmpty(); }

    public LogEntry next() {
        if (!hasNext()) throw new NoSuchElementException();
        
        // 1. Get iterator with smallest current element
        PeekingIterator<LogEntry> shortest = minHeap.poll();
        LogEntry result = shortest.next(); // Consume it
        
        // 2. Put iterator back if it has more data
        if (shortest.hasNext()) {
            minHeap.add(shortest);
        }
        
        return result;
    }
}

// Usage: Merging 3 sorted log streams
public class LogMergeDemo {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        List<LogEntry> log1 = Arrays.asList(new LogEntry(10, "Boot"), new LogEntry(30, "Warn"));
        List<LogEntry> log2 = Arrays.asList(new LogEntry(15, "Connect"), new LogEntry(20, "Auth"));
        List<LogEntry> log3 = Arrays.asList(new LogEntry(5, "Ping"), new LogEntry(50, "Crash"));
        
        List<PeekingIterator<LogEntry>> sources = new ArrayList<>();
        sources.add(new SortedListIterator(log1));
        sources.add(new SortedListIterator(log2));
        sources.add(new SortedListIterator(log3));
        
        MergingIterator merger = new MergingIterator(sources);
        
        while(merger.hasNext()) {
            System.out.println(merger.next());
        }
    }
}
```
**Output**: `5 (Ping) -> 10 (Boot) -> 15 (Connect) -> 20 (Auth) -> 30 (Warn) -> 50 (Crash)`

### **8. Project 5: Infinite Stream Generator (Fibonacci)**

Iterators don't need a backing collection. They can compute values on the fly.
**Safety**: We implement a `TakingIterator` decorator that limits the stream.

```java
import java.math.BigInteger;
import java.util.Iterator;

class FibonacciIterator implements Iterator<BigInteger> {
    private BigInteger curr = BigInteger.ONE;
    private BigInteger prev = BigInteger.ZERO;

    public boolean hasNext() { return true; } // Infinite!

    public BigInteger next() {
        BigInteger temp = curr;
        curr = curr.add(prev);
        prev = temp;
        return prev; // 1, 1, 2, 3, 5...
    }
}

// Decorator: Limits an infinite iterator
class TakingIterator<T> implements Iterator<T> {
    private Iterator<T> source;
    private int remaining;

    public TakingIterator(Iterator<T> source, int limit) {
        this.source = source;
        this.remaining = limit;
    }

    public boolean hasNext() { return remaining > 0 && source.hasNext(); }

    public T next() {
        remaining--;
        return source.next();
    }
}

public class StreamDemo {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        Iterator<BigInteger> infinite = new FibonacciIterator();
        Iterator<BigInteger> limited = new TakingIterator<>(infinite, 10);
        
        while(limited.hasNext()) {
            System.out.print(limited.next() + ", ");
        }
    }
}
```

### **9. Deep Dive: `Spliterator` & Parallel Streams**

Java 8 introduced `Spliterator` (Split-Iterator) to support parallel processing.
Instead of just `next()`, it has `trySplit()`.

**How Parallel Stream Works**:
1.  **Main Thread**: Calls `spliterator.trySplit()`.
2.  **Spliterator**: "I define the range [0, 1000]. I will give you [0, 500] and keep [501, 1000]."
3.  **ForkJoinPool**: Steals the new Spliterator and processes it on another CPU core.

**Key Method**:
```java
public Spliterator<T> trySplit() {
    // If too small, return null (don't split)
    if (this.size < 100) return null; 
    
    // Return a new Spliterator covering half the data
    return new MySpliterator(data, start, mid);
}
```

> [!NOTE]
> **Interview Tip**: If asked "How does `list.parallelStream()` work?", explain **Spliterator** partitioning the data for the ForkJoinPool.

### **12. Multi-Language Perspectives**

| Language | Feature | Description |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Java** | `Iterator<T>`, `Spliterator` | Standard Interface. `Spliterator` powers Parallel Streams. |
| **Python** | `__iter__`, `__next__`, `yield` | Generators (`yield`) make writing iterators trivial. "Lazy Evaluation" is the default. |
| **C++** | `std::vector<T>::iterator` | Pointer arithmetic style (`*it`, `it++`). Zero-overhead abstractions. |
| **JavaScript** | `Symbol.iterator`, `function*` | ES6 introduced Generators and `for...of` loops standardizing iteration. |
| **Go** | `func Next() (value, ok)` | No standard `Iterator` interface (until recent Go versions). Idiomatically uses Channels or Closures. |

**Python Example (Generator)**:
```python
def fibonacci():
    a, b = 0, 1
    while True:
        yield a
        a, b = b, a + b

# Usage
gen = fibonacci()
print(next(gen)) # 0
print(next(gen)) # 1
```

#### Q74: How does the Visitor Pattern enable "Double Dispatch"?
**Companies**: Google (Compilers), Facebook (AST Transformations), IntelliJ IDEA (PsiFiles)
**Difficulty**: **Hard** (Double Dispatch / Cyclic Dependency)
**Category**: Behavioral Patterns, Algorithms

---

### **1. Conceptual Overview & Motivation**

**The "Why": Adding Operations to Locked Classes**

<div style="border: 1px solid #ccc; padding: 10px; margin-bottom: 20px;">
    <strong>Interactive Visualization:</strong>
    <iframe src="vis/visitor_viz.html" width="100%" height="550px" style="border:none;"></iframe>
    <p style="text-align: center; font-size: 12px;"><a href="vis/visitor_viz.html" target="_blank">Open Visualization in New Tab</a></p>
</div>

You have a stable class hierarchy: `Shape`, `Circle`, `Rectangle`.
You want to add a new operation: `exportToXML()`.

**Naive Approach**: Add `exportToXML()` method to `Shape` interface and all subclasses.
**Problem**:
1.  **Violation of SRP**: Shapes should handle geometry, not XML serialization.
2.  **Violation of OCP**: You are modifying existing tested classes.
3.  **Future Bloat**: Next week you need `exportToJSON()`, `exportToYAML()`. The classes grow forever.

**The Solution**: The Visitor Pattern.
Move the operation logic into a separate class (`XmlExportVisitor`).
The Shapes just need *one* method: `accept(Visitor v)`.
When you call `shape.accept(v)`, the shape "calls back" the visitor: `v.visit(this)`.

**Real-World Analogies**:
1.  **Taxi Driver (Visitor)**: Visits different places.
    -   At a **Hotel**: Picks up passenger.
    -   At a **Gas Station**: Refuels.
    -   The places don't know how to drive a taxi; they just "accept" the driver.
2.  **Tax Auditor**: Visits a `Factory` (checks inventory), Visits a `Shop` (checks sales). The logic resides in the Auditor, not the buildings.

### **2. Interactive Visualization: AST Traversal (Double Dispatch)**

This D3.js visualization demonstrates how a Visitor traverses an **Abstract Syntax Tree (AST)** for the math expression `(5 + 3) * 2`.
Observe how the `Visitor` jumps from node to node, and how the **Type** of the node determines which `visit()` method is called.

<div id="visitor-viz" style="border: 1px solid #ccc; padding: 20px; border-radius: 8px; background: #1e1e1e; color: #fff;">
    <svg id="visitor-svg" width="800" height="300"></svg>
    <div style="margin-top: 15px; display: flex; gap: 10px;">
        <button onclick="startVisitor()" style="padding: 8px; background: #4caf50; border: none; color: white; border-radius: 4px; cursor: pointer;">Start Traversal</button>
        <button onclick="resetVisitor()" style="padding: 8px; background: #555; border: none; color: white; border-radius: 4px; cursor: pointer;">Reset</button>
        <div id="visitor-status" style="margin-left: 10px; padding: 8px; font-family: monospace; color: #00bcd4;">Status: Ready</div>
    </div>
    <div id="visitor-code" style="margin-top: 10px; font-family: monospace; font-size: 12px; background: #333; padding: 10px; white-space: pre-wrap; height: 100px; overflow-y: scroll;"></div>
</div>

<script>
    const visitorSvg = d3.select("#visitor-svg");
    
    // AST for (5 + 3) * 2
    const astData = {
        name: "*", type: "Multiply", id: "root",
        children: [
            {
                name: "+", type: "Add", id: "add",
                children: [
                    { name: "5", type: "Literal", id: "lit5" },
                    { name: "3", type: "Literal", id: "lit3" }
                ]
            },
            { name: "2", type: "Literal", id: "lit2" }
        ]
    };

    let visitorRoot = d3.hierarchy(astData);
    let visitorTreeCheck = d3.tree().size([700, 250]);
    visitorTreeCheck(visitorRoot);
    
    const nodes = visitorRoot.descendants();
    const links = visitorRoot.links();
    
    // Draw Links
    visitorSvg.selectAll(".link")
        .data(links)
        .enter().append("path")
        .attr("class", "link")
        .attr("d", d3.linkVertical().x(d => d.x + 50).y(d => d.y + 40))
        .attr("fill", "none")
        .attr("stroke", "#555")
        .attr("stroke-width", 2);

    // Draw Nodes
    const nodeGroup = visitorSvg.selectAll(".node")
        .data(nodes)
        .enter().append("g")
        .attr("class", "node")
        .attr("transform", d => `translate(${d.x + 50},${d.y + 40})`);

    nodeGroup.append("circle")
        .attr("r", 20)
        .attr("fill", d => d.data.type === "Literal" ? "#ff9800" : "#2196f3")
        .attr("stroke", "#fff")
        .attr("id", d => "node-" + d.data.id);

    nodeGroup.append("text")
        .text(d => d.data.name)
        .attr("dy", 5)
        .attr("text-anchor", "middle")
        .attr("fill", "#fff")
        .style("font-weight", "bold");
        
    nodeGroup.append("text")
        .text(d => d.data.type)
        .attr("dy", -25)
        .attr("text-anchor", "middle")
        .attr("fill", "#aaa")
        .style("font-size", "10px");

    // Visitor Token
    const visitorToken = visitorSvg.append("circle")
        .attr("r", 8)
        .attr("fill", "#e91e63")
        .attr("stroke", "#fff")
        .attr("stroke-width", 2)
        .attr("cx", nodes[0].x + 50)
        .attr("cy", nodes[0].y + 40)
        .attr("opacity", 0);

    const steps = [
        { id: "root", msg: "visit(Multiply): Visiting Root. Left child next..." },
        { id: "add", msg: "visit(Add): Visiting Left Child. Left child next..." },
        { id: "lit5", msg: "visit(Literal): Found 5. Returning..." },
        { id: "add", msg: "visit(Add): Back at Add. Right child next..." },
        { id: "lit3", msg: "visit(Literal): Found 3. Returning..." },
        { id: "add", msg: "visit(Add): Calc 5 + 3 = 8. Returning..." },
        { id: "root", msg: "visit(Multiply): Back at Root. Right child next..." },
        { id: "lit2", msg: "visit(Literal): Found 2. Returning..." },
        { id: "root", msg: "visit(Multiply): Calc 8 * 2 = 16. DONE." }
    ];

    function startVisitor() {
        visitorToken.attr("opacity", 1);
        let stepIdx = 0;
        
        function nextStep() {
            if (stepIdx >= steps.length) return;
            
            const step = steps[stepIdx];
            const targetNode = nodes.find(n => n.data.id === step.id);
            
            visitorToken.transition().duration(1000)
                .attr("cx", targetNode.x + 50)
                .attr("cy", targetNode.y + 40)
                .on("end", () => {
                    document.getElementById("visitor-status").innerText = step.msg;
                    document.getElementById("visitor-code").innerText += `> ${step.msg}\n`;
                    document.getElementById("visitor-code").scrollTop = 999;
                    stepIdx++;
                    setTimeout(nextStep, 500);
                });
        }
        document.getElementById("visitor-code").innerText = "";
        nextStep();
    }
    
    function resetVisitor() {
        visitorToken.attr("opacity", 0).attr("cx", nodes[0].x + 50).attr("cy", nodes[0].y + 40);
        document.getElementById("visitor-status").innerText = "Status: Ready";
        document.getElementById("visitor-code").innerText = "";
    }
</script>

### **3. Comprehensive Definition**

**Formal Definition**:
> Represent an operation to be performed on the elements of an object structure. Visitor lets you define a new operation without changing the classes of the elements on which it operates.

**The Key Roles**:
1.  **Visitor Interface**: Declares `visit(ConcreteElementA)`, `visit(ConcreteElementB)`.
2.  **Concrete Visitor**: Implements the operation (e.g., `XmlVisitor`).
3.  **Element Interface**: Declares `accept(Visitor)`.
4.  **Concrete Element**: Implements `accept(v) { v.visit(this); }`.

---

### **4. Progressive Solution Evolution**

#### Approach 1: InstanceOf Checks (The Anti-Pattern)
```java
void export(Shape s) {
    if (s instanceof Circle) exportCircle((Circle) s);
    else if (s instanceof Rect) exportRect((Rect) s);
}
```
*   **Critique**: You lose polymorphism. If you add `Triangle`, this code breaks silently (or requires updating every `if-else` chain).

#### Approach 2: Method Overloading (Static Dispatch)
```java
export(Circle c);
export(Shape s);
// Calling export(myShape) calls export(Shape), NOT export(Circle)!
```
*   **Critique**: Java chooses method overloads at **compile time**. It doesn't know the runtime type.

#### Approach 3: Double Dispatch (Visitor)
1.  Dynamic dispatch on `element.accept(v)` (Selects correct Element).
2.  Dynamic dispatch on `v.visit(this)` (Selects correct Visitor method for that Element).
*   **Verdict**: Correctly routes (Visitor Type, Element Type) -> Method.

---

### **5. Project 1: Enterprise Tax Engine**
**Scenario**: Calculating taxes for a Shopping Cart containing different types of products.
**Requirement**: Support different tax regimes (US, EU, VAT) without modifying product classes.

```java
import java.util.*;

// 1. VISITOR INTERFACE
interface TaxVisitor {
    double visit(Liquor l);
    double visit(Tobacco t);
    double visit(Necessity n);
}

// 2. ELEMENT INTERFACE
interface Item {
    double accept(TaxVisitor v);
}

// 3. CONCRETE ELEMENTS
class Liquor implements Item {
    private double price;
    public Liquor(double price) { this.price = price; }
    public double getPrice() { return price; }
    public double accept(TaxVisitor v) { return v.visit(this); }
}

class Tobacco implements Item {
    private double price;
    public Tobacco(double price) { this.price = price; }
    public double getPrice() { return price; }
    public double accept(TaxVisitor v) { return v.visit(this); }
}

class Necessity implements Item {
    private double price;
    public Necessity(double price) { this.price = price; }
    public double getPrice() { return price; }
    public double accept(TaxVisitor v) { return v.visit(this); }
}

// 4. CONCRETE VISITORS
class UsTaxVisitor implements TaxVisitor {
    public double visit(Liquor l) { return l.getPrice() * 0.18; }
    public double visit(Tobacco t) { return t.getPrice() * 0.32; }
    public double visit(Necessity n) { return 0; } // Tax free
}

class EuVatVisitor implements TaxVisitor {
    public double visit(Liquor l) { return l.getPrice() * 0.22; }
    public double visit(Tobacco t) { return t.getPrice() * 0.50; } // High tax
    public double visit(Necessity n) { return l.getPrice() * 0.05; }
}

public class TaxDemo {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        List<Item> cart = Arrays.asList(new Liquor(100), new Tobacco(50), new Necessity(20));
        
        TaxVisitor usVisitor = new UsTaxVisitor();
        TaxVisitor euVisitor = new EuVatVisitor();
        
        double usTotal = 0, euTotal = 0;
        
        for (Item item : cart) {
            usTotal += item.accept(usVisitor);
            euTotal += item.accept(euVisitor);
        }
        
        System.out.println("US Tax Total: " + usTotal);
        System.out.println("EU Tax Total: " + euTotal);
    }
}
```


// 5. USAGE
public class VisitorDemo {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        TaxVisitor holidayCalc = new HolidayTaxVisitor();
        
        List<Item> cart = new ArrayList<>();
        cart.add(new Liquor(100)); // 10
        cart.add(new Tobacco(50)); // 15
        cart.add(new Necessity(20)); // 0
        
        double totalTax = 0;
        for (Item item : cart) {
            totalTax += item.accept(holidayCalc);
        }
        System.out.println("Total Tax: " + totalTax);
    }
}
```

### **6. Project 2: AST Code Analyzer (Static Analysis)**

**Scenario**: You are building a **Linter** (like SonarQube or ESLint).
**The Structure**: Source code is parsed into an AST (`ClassNode`, `MethodNode`, `VariableNode`).
**The Operation**: Calculate metrics (Cyclomatic Complexity) or find bugs (Unused Variables) without changing the AST nodes.

```java
import java.util.*;

// 1. AST NODES
interface AstNode {
    void accept(AstVisitor v);
}

class ClassNode implements AstNode {
    String name;
    List<MethodNode> methods = new ArrayList<>();
    public ClassNode(String name) { this.name = name; }
    public void accept(AstVisitor v) { v.visit(this); }
}

class MethodNode implements AstNode {
    String name;
    int linesOfCode;
    public MethodNode(String name, int lines) { this.name = name; this.linesOfCode = lines; }
    public void accept(AstVisitor v) { v.visit(this); }
}

class VariableNode implements AstNode {
    String name;
    boolean isUsed = false;
    public VariableNode(String name) { this.name = name; }
    public void accept(AstVisitor v) { v.visit(this); }
}

// 2. VISITOR INTERFACE
interface AstVisitor {
    void visit(ClassNode c);
    void visit(MethodNode m);
    void visit(VariableNode v);
}

// 3. CONCRETE VISITOR: Cyclomatic Complexity & Quality Metrics
class QualityMetricsVisitor implements AstVisitor {
    private int totalLines = 0;
    private int methodCount = 0;
    
    @Override
    public void visit(ClassNode c) {
        System.out.println("Analyzing Class: " + c.name);
        for (MethodNode m : c.methods) {
            m.accept(this); // Recursive visit
        }
    }

    @Override
    public void visit(MethodNode m) {
        methodCount++;
        totalLines += m.linesOfCode;
        if (m.linesOfCode > 50) {
            System.out.println("⚠️ Warning: Method '" + m.name + "' is too large (" + m.linesOfCode + " lines).");
        }
    }

    @Override
    public void visit(VariableNode v) {
        // No-op for metrics
    }
    
    public void printReport() {
        System.out.println("--- Quality Report ---");
        System.out.println("Total Methods: " + methodCount);
        System.out.println("Avg LOC/Method: " + (methodCount == 0 ? 0 : totalLines / methodCount));
    }
}

// 4. CONCRETE VISITOR: Detect Unused Variables
class DeadCodeVisitor implements AstVisitor {
    @Override
    public void visit(ClassNode c) {
        for (MethodNode m : c.methods) m.accept(this);
    }
    
    @Override
    public void visit(MethodNode m) {
        // Pseudo-logic: traverse body to find vars
    }
    
    @Override
    public void visit(VariableNode v) {
        if (!v.isUsed) {
            System.out.println("❌ Error: Variable '" + v.name + "' is never used!");
        }
    }
}

public class LinterDemo {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        ClassNode clazz = new ClassNode("UserService");
        MethodNode m1 = new MethodNode("login", 20);
        MethodNode m2 = new MethodNode("complexAlgo", 150); // Too big!
        
        clazz.methods.add(m1);
        clazz.methods.add(m2);
        
        QualityMetricsVisitor qualityCheck = new QualityMetricsVisitor();
        clazz.accept(qualityCheck);
        
        qualityCheck.printReport();
    }
}
```

> [!TIP]
> **Recursive Traversal**: Notice how `visit(ClassNode)` manually iterates its children (`m.accept(this)`). This is a common pattern when the Visitor handles the traversal logic.

### **7. Project 3: Universal Document Exporter**

**Scenario**: A Google Doc structure (`Page`, `Paragraph`, `Image`, `Table`).
**Requirement**: Export to PDF, HTML, and Markdown.

```java
// ELEMENTS
interface DocElement { void accept(Exporter v); }

class Paragraph implements DocElement {
    String text;
    public Paragraph(String t) { this.text = t; }
    public void accept(Exporter v) { v.visit(this); }
}

class Image implements DocElement {

    public Image(String s) { this.src = s; }
    public void accept(Exporter v) { v.visit(this); }
}

class Hyperlink implements DocElement {
    String url;
    public Hyperlink(String u) { this.url = u; }
    public void accept(Exporter v) { v.visit(this); }
}

// VISITOR
interface Exporter {
    void visit(Paragraph p);
    void visit(Image i);
    void visit(Hyperlink h);
}

class HtmlExporter implements Exporter {
    public void visit(Paragraph p) { System.out.println("<p>" + p.text + "</p>"); }
    public void visit(Image i) { System.out.println("<img src='" + i.src + "' />"); }
    public void visit(Hyperlink h) { System.out.println("<a href='" + h.url + "'>link</a>"); }
}

class MarkdownExporter implements Exporter {
    public void visit(Paragraph p) { System.out.println(p.text + "\n"); }
    public void visit(Image i) { System.out.println("![](" + i.src + ")"); }

class ZipVisitor implements FileSystemVisitor {
    public void visit(FileNode file) {
        System.out.println("Compressing " + file.name + " (" + file.size + "kb) -> " + (file.size/2) + "kb");
    }
    public void visit(DirectoryNode dir) {

        for(Node child : dir.children) child.accept(this);

### **10. Deep Dive: The Expression Problem**

**The Core Computer Science Problem**:
> "How can we define a datatype and add new cases to it (new Classes) OR add new functions to it (new Methods) without recompiling existing code?"

1.  **OOP (Java)**: Easy to add new **Classes** (`Triangle`, `Hexagon`). Hard to add new **Methods** (`exportXML`) to all classes.
2.  **Functional (Haskell/ML)**: Easy to add new **Functions**. Hard to add new **Data Types** (requires updating all functions).

**Visitor Pattern** flips the table for OOP. It makes Java behave like a Functional language:
-   **Easy**: Add new Operations (just make a new Visitor).
-   **Hard**: Add new Classes (must break the `Visitor` interface).

**Takeaway**: Use Visitor when your **Data Structure (Classes)** is stable, but algorithms acting on it evolve frequently.

---

### **11. Modern Java: 17+ Pattern Matching (Visitor Killer?)**

Java 17 (EP 406) introduced `switch` pattern matching, which solves the Double Dispatch problem cleanly without the Visitor boiler-plate.

**The "Old" Visitor Way**:
```java
// Requires interfaces, accept(), visit(), concrete visitors... 
circle.accept(new XmlVisitor());
```

**The Modern Java Way**:
```java
public String exportToXml(Shape shape) {
    return switch (shape) {
        case Circle c    -> "<circle r='" + c.radius() + "' />";
        case Rect r      -> "<rect w='" + r.w() + "' h='" + r.h() + "' />";
        case Triangle t  -> "<poly points='" + t.points() + "' />";
        // If Shape is 'sealed', compiler checks exhaustiveness!
    };
}
```
**Pros**:
-   No `accept`/`visit` methods.
-   Logic is centralized in one method, not scattered classes.
-   Combines well with **Sealed Classes**.

**Cons**:
-   Not fully OOP (polymorphism). It's "Type Inspection".
-   If `Shape` is in a library you can't control (and not sealed), you might miss cases.

---

### **12. Security Analysis: Recursion Bombs & Cycles**

1.  **Stack Overflow**: Visitors often recurse (`dir.accept(this)` -> `child.accept(this)`).
    -   **Attack**: User uploads a JSON with 10,000 nested arrays.
    -   **Mitigation**: Implement `MaxDepth` counter in the Visitor.
2.  **Infinite Loops (Cycles)**: A directory containing a Symlink to itself.
    -   **Mitigation**: Maintain a `Set<Node> visited`. If `visited.contains(current)`, stop.

---

### **13. Interview Defense**

**Q1: Why not just use `instanceof`?**
> "In huge systems (compilers), `instanceof` chains are slow (O(N) checks) and fragile. If I add a node type, I have to grep the entire codebase to find all `if-else` chains. Visitor gives me compile-time safety (if I add a node to the Interface, the compiler forces me to update all Visitors)."

**Q2: What is Double Dispatch?**
> "It's when the method executed depends on the runtime type of *two* objects: the Receiver and the Argument. Java only supports Single Dispatch (Receiver only). Visitor simulates Double Dispatch by making two calls: `element.accept(v)` and `v.visit(element)`."

**Q3: Can a Visitor return a value?**
> "Standard `void visit()` doesn't, forcing you to store state in the Visitor field. However, you can make a generic `Visitor<R>` where `R visit()` returns a result."

---

### **14. Cheatsheet & Summary**

| Metric | Visitor Pattern |
| :--- | :--- |
| **Primary Use** | ASTs, Document Export, Compilers. |
| **Pros** | SRP (Separates Algorithm from Data), Double Dispatch. |
| **Cons** | Hard to add new Element types. Verbose. |
| **Modern Alt** | Java 17 Sealed Classes + Pattern Matching (Switch). |

### **15. Multi-Language Perspectives (Beyond Java)**

1.  **Scala**: Pattern Matching.
    ```scala
    def interpret(node: Node): Int = node match {
      case Number(n) => n
      case Add(l, r) => interpret(l) + interpret(r)
    }
    ```
    *No Visitor needed.*

2.  **Rust**: Enums + Match.
    ```rust
    enum Expr { Num(i32), Add(Box<Expr>, Box<Expr>) }
    fn interpret(e: Expr) -> i32 {
        match e {
            Expr::Num(n) => n,
            Expr::Add(l, r) => interpret(*l) + interpret(*r),
        }
    }
    ```

3.  **Go**: Type Switches.
    ```go
    func interpret(n Node) int {
        switch v := n.(type) {
        case Number: return v.Val
        case BinOp:  return interpret(v.Left) + interpret(v.Right)
        }
    }
    ```

#### Q75: How does the Composite Pattern allow treating Leaf and Node uniformly?
**Companies**: Amazon (S3 Objects), Microsoft (File Explorer), React (Virtual DOM), Adobe (Layers)
**Difficulty**: **Hard** (Recursion / Generics / Cycle Detection)
**Category**: Structural Patterns, Trees

---

### **1. Conceptual Overview & Motivation**

<div style="border: 1px solid #ccc; padding: 10px; margin-bottom: 20px;">
    <strong>Interactive Visualization:</strong>
    <iframe src="vis/composite_viz.html" width="100%" height="540px" style="border:none;"></iframe>
    <p style="text-align: center; font-size: 12px;"><a href="vis/composite_viz.html" target="_blank">Open Visualization in New Tab</a></p>
</div>

**The "Why": The Part-Whole Hierarchy Problem**
Imagine you are building a **Drawing App**.
*   You have **Primitives**: `Line`, `Circle`, `Square`.
*   You have **Groups**: A `Car` is a Group containing 2 Circles (Wheels) and 1 Square (Body).
*   You have **Meta-Groups**: A `TrafficJam` is a Group containing 50 `Car` groups.

**The Problem**:
If you treat them differently:
```java
public void draw(Object o) {
    if (o instanceof Shape) ((Shape)o).draw();
    else if (o instanceof Group) {
        for (Object child : ((Group)o).getChildren()) draw(child); // Recursive logic leaking
    }
}
```
Client code becomes a mess of `instanceof` checks. You can't easily rotate, resize, or move "everything" without knowing its internal structure.

**The Solution**: The Composite Pattern.
Define a common interface `Component` (e.g., `Graphic`).
*   `Leaf` (Circle): Implements `draw()`.
*   `Composite` (Group): Implements `draw()` by calling `draw()` on all children.
*   **Uniformity**: The client just calls `graphic.draw()`. It doesn't care if it's a single dot or a blueprint of the Death Star.

---

### **2. Comprehensive Definition**

**Formal Definition**:
> Compose objects into tree structures to represent part-whole hierarchies. Composite lets clients treat individual objects and compositions of objects uniformly.

**Key Components**:
1.  **Component**: The abstraction (`FileSystemNode`, `UIWidget`).
2.  **Leaf**: Building blocks (`File`, `Button`). Has NO children.
3.  **Composite**: Aggregates components (`Folder`, `Panel`). Delegates operations recursively.

---

### **3. Progressive Solution Evolution**

#### Approach 1: Type Checking (The Anti-Pattern)
Using `instanceof` to distinguish Lists from Objects.
*   **Critique**: Violates Open-Closed Principle. New types require changing all client logic.

#### Approach 2: The "Container" Inheritance (Fragile)
`class Folder extends File`?
*   **Critique**: Conceptually wrong. A Folder IS NOT a File (Liskov Substitution Principle violation if File has `byte[] content`).

#### Approach 3: Composite (Polymorphic Tree)
Both `File` and `Folder` implement `IFileSystem`.
*   **Verdict**: The Standard Solution. Enables recursive algorithms.

---

### **4. Project 1: Enterprise UI Component System (Virtual DOM)**
**Scenario**: Building a React-like rendering engine where a `Page` contains `Panels`, which contain `Buttons` and `Text`.

```java
import java.util.ArrayList;
import java.util.List;
import java.util.stream.Collectors;

// 1. COMPONENT
interface UIComponent {
    String render();
}

// 2. LEAF (Atomic Elements)
class Button implements UIComponent {
    private String label;
    public Button(String label) { this.label = label; }
    
    @Override
    public String render() {
        return "<button>" + label + "</button>";
    }
}

class TextSpan implements UIComponent {
    private String text;
    public TextSpan(String text) { this.text = text; }
    
    @Override
    public String render() {
        return "<span>" + text + "</span>";
    }
}

// 3. COMPOSITE (Containers)
class DivPanel implements UIComponent {
    private List<UIComponent> children = new ArrayList<>();
    private String className;

    public DivPanel(String className) { this.className = className; }

    public void add(UIComponent c) { children.add(c); }

    @Override
    public String render() {
        String content = children.stream()
            .map(UIComponent::render)
            .collect(Collectors.joining(""));
        return "<div class='" + className + "'>" + content + "</div>";
    }
}

// 4. USAGE
public class VirtualDomDemo {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        DivPanel card = new DivPanel("card");
        DivPanel header = new DivPanel("card-header");
        DivPanel body = new DivPanel("card-body");

        header.add(new TextSpan("User Profile"));
        body.add(new TextSpan("Name: Alice"));
        body.add(new Button("Edit"));

        card.add(header);
        card.add(body);

        System.out.println(card.render());
        // Output: <div class='card'><div class='card-header'><span>User Profile</span></div><div class='card-body'><span>Name: Alice</span><button>Edit</button></div></div>
    }
}
```

### **5. Project 2: Distributed File System (DFS) with Quotas**
**Scenario**: Calculating directory sizes where some folders might be **Symlinks** or **Mount Points** to other servers.

```java
// COMPONENT
abstract class DFSNode {
    String name;
    public DFSNode(String name) { this.name = name; }
    
    public abstract long getSize(); // The polymorphic magic
}

// LEAF
class DFSFile extends DFSNode {
    private long sizeBytes;
    public DFSFile(String name, long size) {
        super(name);
        this.sizeBytes = size;
    }
    @Override
    public long getSize() { return sizeBytes; }
}

// COMPOSITE
class DFSDirectory extends DFSNode {
    private List<DFSNode> children = new ArrayList<>();
    private Map<String, Long> cache = new java.util.HashMap<>(); // Cache sizes

    public DFSDirectory(String name) { super(name); }
    public void add(DFSNode node) { children.add(node); }

    @Override
    public long getSize() {
        // Simple recursive sum (Production would use Caching)
        return children.stream().mapToLong(DFSNode::getSize).sum();
    }
}

// PROXY / COMPOSITE HYBRID (Mount Point)
class RemoteMountPoint extends DFSNode {
    private String remoteUrl;
    public RemoteMountPoint(String name, String url) { 
        super(name); 
        this.remoteUrl = url;
    }

    @Override
    public long getSize() {
        // Simulate network call
        System.out.println("Connecting to " + remoteUrl + "..."); 
        return 5000; // Mocked size
    }
}
```

### **6. Deep Dive: Transparent vs Safe**

**The Dilemma**: Where do you declare `add()`, `remove()`, `getChild()`?

| Feature | Transparency (In Component) | Safety (In Composite Only) |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Location** | `Component` Interface | `Composite` Class |
| **Leaf Impl** | Throws `UnsupportedOperationException` | Method doesn't exist |
| **Client Code** | `node.add(child)` (Clean) | `if (node instanceof Composite) ((Composite)node).add()` (Messy) |
| **Runtime Safety** | Low (Runtime Exception possible) | High (Compile-time check) |
| **Usage** | UI Frameworks (Generic Trees) | Internal Domain Models (Stricter types) |

> **Senior SDE Tip**: Most modern frameworks prefer **Transparency** for Read operations (`getSize`, `render`) but **Safety** for Write operations (`add`, `remove`).

**Scenario**: Propagate a company-wide bonus.
*   **Leaf**: `IndividualContributor` (Gets bonus directly).

interface Employee {
    void payBonus(double percent);
}

class Developer implements Employee {
    String name;
    double salary;
    public Developer(String n, double s) { name = n; salary = s; }

class Manager implements Employee {
    String name;
    List<Employee> team = new ArrayList<>();
    
    public void add(Employee e) { team.add(e); }

        for(Employee e : team) e.payBonus(percent); 
    }
}

### **8. Amazon Leadership Principles & Interview Defense**

**"Invent and Simplify"**
> *Candidate*: "I used the **Composite Pattern** to simplify the config loader. Instead of writing separate parsers for JSON objects and JSON arrays, I treated everything as a `JsonNode`. This allowed me to write a single recursive validator that worked for validitating a single field or a nested list of 1000 objects."

**"Dive Deep"**
> *Candidate*: "I had to handle **Cyclic Graphs**. Users could create symlinks that pointed to parent folders, causing infinite recursion in `getSize()`. I solved this by passing a `Set<Node> visited` context down the recursion stack to detect loops."

### **9. Multi-Language Perspectives**

*   **Java**: Standard `interface` or `abstract class`.
*   **C++**: `std::vector<std::shared_ptr<Component>>`. Must watch out for circular `shared_ptr` (Memory Leaks). Use `std::weak_ptr` for parent back-references.
*   **Rust**: `Vec<Box<dyn Component>>`. Ownership is strict. A Component cannot easily own its parent (RefCell/Rc cycles).
*   **Python**: Duck typing makes Composite trivial. `def operation(self):` just works on both lists and items.

interface QueryNode {
    String toSql();
}

class Condition implements QueryNode { // LEAF
    String term;
    public Condition(String t) { term = t; }
    public String toSql() { return term; }
}

class AndGroup implements QueryNode { // COMPOSITE
    List<QueryNode> nodes = new ArrayList<>();
    public void add(QueryNode n) { nodes.add(n); }
    public String toSql() {
        return "(" + nodes.stream().map(QueryNode::toSql).collect(Collectors.joining(" AND ")) + ")";
    }
}

### **11. Project 5: Build Tool Dependency Graph (Cycle Detection)**
**Scenario**: Detecting circular dependencies in a multi-module project (e.g., Maven/Gradle).

```java
class BuildModule {
    String name;
    List<BuildModule> dependencies = new ArrayList<>();
    boolean visited = false;
    boolean onStack = false; // For cycle detection

    public BuildModule(String n) { name = n; }
    public void addDep(BuildModule m) { dependencies.add(m); }

    public void build() {
        if (onStack) throw new RuntimeException("Cycle Detected: " + name);
        if (visited) return;
        
        onStack = true;
        for (BuildModule dep : dependencies) dep.build();
        
        System.out.println("Building " + name);
        onStack = false;
        visited = true;
    }
}
```

### **12. Security Analysis: Recursive DoS**

**Vulnerability**: Recursive Stack Overflow.
If an attacker can create a deeply nested structure (e.g., a "Zip Bomb" of nested folders or a JSON with 10k nested objects), calling `composite.operation()` will blow the Stack (`StackOverflowError`).

**Mitigation**:
1.  **Limit Recursion Depth**: pass `depth` param and throw if > 500.
2.  **Iterative Traversal**: Use a `Stack<Node>` or `Queue<Node>` in the heap instead of the call stack.

```java
// Safe Iterative Traversal
public void traverseSafe(Node root) {
    Stack<Node> stack = new Stack<>();
    stack.push(root);
    while(!stack.isEmpty()) {
        Node current = stack.pop();
        process(current);
        // Add children to stack
        for(Node child : current.getChildren()) stack.push(child);
    }
}
```

---

### **13. Cheatsheet & Summary**

| Pattern | Structure | Key Benefit |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Composite** | `Tree` | Uniform leaf/node handling. |
| **Decorator** | `Wrapper` | Adding behavior dynamically. |
| **Chain** | `List` | Decoupling sender/receiver. |

**Verdict**: Use Composite whenever you have "Part-Whole" hierarchies and want to ignore the difference between single and groups. But beware of **Recursion Depth** and **Cycles**!

### **SECTION 1: QUESTION ANALYSIS & UNDERSTANDING**

#### 📋 Question Statement
**"Design and implement an Interpreter pattern to evaluate a custom language grammar. Your solution must handle context variables, operator precedence, and nested expressions. Additionally, provide a security analysis of your implementation."**

#### 🎯 Question Analysis
This question is a favorite at FAANG for Senior/Staff roles because it filters candidates who only know "API coding" from those who understand computer science fundamentals (Compilers, Recursion, Trees).

**What This Question Really Tests**:
1.  **Recursion & Trees**: Can you navigate an Abstract Syntax Tree (AST)?
2.  **Formal Grammars**: Do you understand BNF (Backus-Naur Form)?
3.  **Design Patterns**: Can you decouple the *grammar* from the *interpretation*?
4.  **Security Mindset**: Do you know about ReDoS or StackOverflow vulnerabilities?

**Difficulty Breakdown**:
*   **Algorithmic Complexity**: **Medium**. The traversal is simple DFS (Depth First Search).
*   **Implementation Complexity**: **Hard**. Building the AST correctly (Parsing) is often harder than the Interpreter itself.
*   **Edge Case Handling**: **Critical**. Infinite loops, cycle detection, and malformed inputs.

**Company-Specific Context**:
*   **Google**: Used in Search Query processing (`site:github.com AND lang:java`).
*   **Amazon**: Used in Config Rules (`IF instance.type == 't2.micro' THEN alert()`).
*   **Microsoft**: Excel formula engine is a massive Interpreter.
*   **Elastic**: The Query DSL (JSON-based) is interpreted into Lucene queries.

### **SECTION 2: SOLUTION PROGRESSION - BRUTE FORCE TO OPTIMAL**

#### 🚀 Solution Evolution Journey

### Approach 1: Brute Force (String Parsing & Splitting)
**Thought Process**:
"I need to evaluate `A AND B`. I can just `split(' AND ')` the string and check both sides."

**Implementation (Anti-Pattern)**:
```java
public boolean bruteForceEvaluate(String expression, Map<String, Boolean> context) {
    // ❌ WRONG: Fails on nested logic like "(A OR B) AND C"
    if (expression.contains(" OR ")) {
        String[] parts = expression.split(" OR ");
        return bruteForceEvaluate(parts[0], context) || bruteForceEvaluate(parts[1], context);
    }
    if (expression.contains(" AND ")) {
        String[] parts = expression.split(" AND ");
        return bruteForceEvaluate(parts[0], context) && bruteForceEvaluate(parts[1], context);
    }
    return context.getOrDefault(expression.trim(), false);
}
```

**Critique**:
*   **Brittle**: Fails completely on parentheses `(A OR B)`.
*   **Precedence Issues**: `A OR B AND C` is ambiguous without a parser.
*   **Scalability**: Adding new operators (`NOT`, `XOR`) creates spaghetti code.

---

### Approach 2: The optimal Interpreter Pattern (AST-Based)
#### 📊 Interactive Visualization
<iframe src="vis/interpreter_viz.html" width="100%" height="500px" style="border:none; background:white;"></iframe>
*Interact with the AST to see how nodes evaluate recursively.*

**Optimization Strategy**:
Instead of hacking strings, we convert the sentence into an **Abstract Syntax Tree (AST)**.
*   **Leaf Nodes (Terminals)**: The variables or constants (`"A"`, `5`).
*   **Composite Nodes (Non-Terminals)**: The operations (`AND`, `OR`, `PLUS`).

**Visualizing the AST**:
For `age > 18 AND isStudent`:
```
      AND
     /   \
    >    isStudent
   / \
 age  18
```

#### 📊 Interactive Visualization
<iframe src="vis/interpreter_viz.html" width="100%" height="500px" style="border:none; background:white;"></iframe>
*Interact with the AST to see how nodes evaluate recursively.*

**Implementation**:

```java
import java.util.*;

/**
 * 1. THE CONTEXT
 * Holds global state (variables, database row, environment).
 */
class Context {
    private Map<String, Object> variables = new HashMap<>();

    public void set(String name, Object value) {
        variables.put(name, value);
    }

    public Object get(String name) {
        return variables.get(name);
    }
}

/**
 * 2. THE ABSTRACT EXPRESSION
 * Verified Senior SDE: Note the use of Generics for type safety.
 */
interface Expression<T> {
    T interpret(Context context);
}

/**
 * 3. TERMINAL EXPRESSION (Leaf Node)
 * Represents a variable lookup.
 */
class VariableExpression implements Expression<Integer> {
    private String name;

    public VariableExpression(String name) {
        this.name = name;
    }

    @Override
    public Integer interpret(Context context) {
        // Detailed Error Handling for missing variables
        Object val = context.get(name);
        if (val == null) throw new RuntimeException("Undefined variable: " + name);
        if (!(val instanceof Integer)) throw new RuntimeException("Variable " + name + " is not an Integer");
        return (Integer) val;
    }
}

class NumberExpression implements Expression<Integer> {
    private int number;
    public NumberExpression(int number) { this.number = number; }
    
    @Override
    public Integer interpret(Context ctx) { return number; }
}

/**
 * 4. NON-TERMINAL EXPRESSION (Composite Node)
 * Represents addition (+).
 */
class AddExpression implements Expression<Integer> {
    private Expression<Integer> left;
    private Expression<Integer> right;

    public AddExpression(Expression<Integer> left, Expression<Integer> right) {
        this.left = left;
        this.right = right;
    }

    @Override
    public Integer interpret(Context context) {
        // Recursively interpret children
        return left.interpret(context) + right.interpret(context);
    }
}

class MultiplyExpression implements Expression<Integer> {
    private Expression<Integer> left;
    private Expression<Integer> right;

    public MultiplyExpression(Expression<Integer> left, Expression<Integer> right) {
        this.left = left;
        this.right = right;
    }

    @Override
    public Integer interpret(Context context) {
        return left.interpret(context) * right.interpret(context);
    }
}

/**
 * 5. CLIENT CODE
 */
public class InterpreterDemo {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        // Goal: Evaluate "price + (tax * 2)"
        
        // 1. Build the AST (Abstract Syntax Tree)
        // In a real app, a Parser would build this. Here we build manually.
        // Tree: Add(Var("price"), Multiply(Var("tax"), Num(2)))
        Expression<Integer> taxExpr = new VariableExpression("tax");
        Expression<Integer> twoExpr = new NumberExpression(2);
        Expression<Integer> multExpr = new MultiplyExpression(taxExpr, twoExpr);
        
        Expression<Integer> priceExpr = new VariableExpression("price");
        Expression<Integer> root = new AddExpression(priceExpr, multExpr);
        
        // 2. Prepare Context
        Context ctx = new Context();
        ctx.set("price", 100);
        ctx.set("tax", 10);
        
        // 3. Interpret
        System.out.println("Result: " + root.interpret(ctx)); // 120
    }
}
```

**Complexity Analysis**:
*   **Time Complexity**: **O(N)** where N is the number of nodes in the AST. We visit each node once.
*   **Space Complexity**: **O(H)** for the recursion stack, where H is the height of the tree. In the worst case (unbalanced tree), O(N).
*   **Why This Is Optimal**: It completely decouples the *grammar* from the *logic*. You can add new operators (e.g., `MinusExpression`) without changing existing code (Open/Closed Principle).

### **SECTION 3: MULTI-LANGUAGE IMPLEMENTATIONS**

#### 🌐 Cross-Language Excellence

### Java Implementation (Generics & Functional)
*See Approach 2 above for the core Class-based implementation.*

**Modern Variation (Java 17+ Records & Sealed Types)**:
```java
// Sealed interface prevents unauthorized extensions (Security)
sealed interface Expr permits Num, Var, Add, Mult {}

record Num(int val) implements Expr {}
record Var(String name) implements Expr {}
record Add(Expr left, Expr right) implements Expr {}
record Mult(Expr left, Expr right) implements Expr {}

// Pattern Matching for Switch (Java 21)
public int evaluate(Expr e, Map<String, Integer> ctx) {
    return switch (e) {
        case Num(var v) -> v;
        case Var(var n) -> ctx.getOrDefault(n, 0);
        case Add(var l, var r) -> evaluate(l, ctx) + evaluate(r, ctx);
        case Mult(var l, var r) -> evaluate(l, ctx) * evaluate(r, ctx);
    };
}
```

### C++ Implementation (Templates & Virtual Functions)
C++ allows highly optimized recursive structures.

```cpp
#include <iostream>
#include <string>
#include <map>
#include <memory>

// Forward Declaration
struct Context { std::map<std::string, int> vars; };

struct Expression {
    virtual int interpret(Context& ctx) = 0;
    virtual ~Expression() = default;
};

struct Number : Expression {
    int val;
    Number(int v) : val(v) {}
    int interpret(Context& ctx) override { return val; }
};

struct Variable : Expression {
    std::string name;
    Variable(std::string n) : name(n) {}
    int interpret(Context& ctx) override { return ctx.vars[name]; }
};

struct Add : Expression {
    std::unique_ptr<Expression> left, right;
    Add(std::unique_ptr<Expression> l, std::unique_ptr<Expression> r) 
        : left(std::move(l)), right(std::move(r)) {}
        
    int interpret(Context& ctx) override {
        return left->interpret(ctx) + right->interpret(ctx);
    }
};
// Usage: unique_ptr ensures no memory leaks for the tree.
```

### Python Implementation (AST Module vs eval)
Python has a built-in `ast` module that parses Python code into an AST.

```python
import ast
import operator

# Safe Evaluator using Python's AST
class SafeEvaluator(ast.NodeVisitor):
    def __init__(self):
        self.operators = {
            ast.Add: operator.add,
            ast.Sub: operator.sub,
            ast.Mult: operator.mul,
            ast.Div: operator.truediv
        }

    def eval(self, expr_str):
        tree = ast.parse(expr_str, mode='eval')
        return self.visit(tree.body)

    def visit_BinOp(self, node):
        left = self.visit(node.left)
        right = self.visit(node.right)
        op_type = type(node.op)
        if op_type not in self.operators:
            raise ValueError(f"Unsupported operator: {op_type}")
        return self.operators[op_type](left, right)

    def visit_Constant(self, node):
        return node.value

# Usage
# print(SafeEvaluator().eval("1 + 2 * 3")) # 7
```
**Warning**: Never use `eval()` on untrusted input. It allows Arbitrary Code Execution (ACE).

### JavaScript/TypeScript Implementation
JSON-based Logic Engines are common in frontend (e.g., specific rules for UI visibility).

```typescript
type Expr = 
  | { type: 'num', val: number }
  | { type: 'var', name: string }
  | { type: 'op', op: '+' | '*', left: Expr, right: Expr };

function interpret(e: Expr, ctx: Record<string, number>): number {
    switch (e.type) {
        case 'num': return e.val;
        case 'var': return ctx[e.name] || 0;
        case 'op':
            const l = interpret(e.left, ctx);
            const r = interpret(e.right, ctx);
            return e.op === '+' ? l + r : l * r;
    }
}
```

### Go Implementation
Go's `text/template` package is a famous standard library interpreter.

```go
// Stringer interface for printing AST
type Node interface {
    Eval(ctx map[string]int) int
}

type AddNode struct { Left, Right Node }

func (n AddNode) Eval(ctx map[string]int) int {
    return n.Left.Eval(ctx) + n.Right.Eval(ctx)
}
// Go emphasizes explicit interfaces and composition over inheritance.
```

### **SECTION 4: EDGE CASES & ERROR HANDLING**

#### 🛡️ Bulletproof Implementation

### Comprehensive Edge Case Analysis

#### 1. Recursion Depth (Stack Overflow)
**Vulnerability**: An attacker sends deeply nested JSON or expression: `(1+(1+(1+...)))`.
**Impact**: Application crash (StackOverflowError).
**Mitigation**:
```java
// Java: Limit depth
public int interpret(Context ctx, int depth) {
    if (depth > 100) throw new SecurityException("Expression too deep");
    // ...
}
```

#### 2. Infinite Loops (Cycles)
**Vulnerability**: If your language supports references (like Excel cells `A1 = B1 + 1`, `B1 = A1`), you can create cycles.
**Impact**: CPU running at 100% until timeout.
**Mitigation**:
*   Pass a `Set<Node> visited` to the interpret method.
*   If `visited.contains(current)`, throw `CycleDetectedException`.

#### 3. ReDoS (Regex Denial of Service)
**Vulnerability**: Interpreting Regex with nested quantifiers `(a+)+`.
**Impact**: Exponential backtracking time O(2^N).
**Mitigation**:
*   Use libraries like Google's RE2 (Linear time).
*   Set a strict timeout for the interpretation thread.

### Error Handling Strategies
**Defensive Programming**:
```java
try {
    result = root.interpret(ctx);
} catch (ArithmeticException e) {
    log.error("Division by zero in rule", e);
    return DEFAULT_VALUE;
} catch (MissingVariableException e) {
    // Graceful degradation
    return 0; 
}
```

### Whiteboard Coding Strategy
**Step 1: Clarify (2 min)**
> *Candidate*: "Before I design the Interpreter, I'd like to clarify the grammar. Are we supporting just boolean logic (`AND`, `OR`), or also comparisons (`>`, `=`)? What about parentheses?"
> *Interviewer*: "Support all of them, including nested parentheses."

**Step 2: Design (5 min)**
> *Candidate*: "I'll use the **Composite Pattern** to structure the AST. A base `Expression` interface will have two implementations: `TerminalExpression` for variables/constants, and `NonTerminalExpression` for operators. I'll use a `Context` object to pass variable values during interpretation."

**Step 3: Implementation (15 min)**
*   Define `Expression<T>` interface.
*   Implement `AndExpression`, `OrExpression`.
*   Show the usage in `main()`.

**Step 4: Testing (5 min)**
> *Candidate*: "I'll trace the execution with `A AND (B OR C)`. If A=True, B=False, C=True:
> 1. `OrExpression(B, C)` evaluates to `False || True` -> `True`.
> 2. `AndExpression(A, Result1)` evaluates to `True && True` -> `True`.
> The logic holds."

### Communication Excellence
*   **Explain Trade-offs**: "I chose Interpreter because the grammar is simple. If we needed a full programming language with loops and functions, I'd suggest a proper Compiler approach or embedding Lua/Python."
*   **Handling Hints**: If the interviewer asks about performance, immediately pivot to **Visitor Pattern** or **Bytecode Generation**.

### **SECTION 6: ADVANCED OPTIMIZATIONS & VARIATIONS**

#### 🚀 Expert-Level Enhancements

### 1. Visitor Pattern Integration
**Problem**: Adding new operations (e.g., "Pretty Print", "Type Check", "Optimize") requires modifying every Expression class.
**Solution**: Use the **Visitor Pattern** to separate operations from the structure.

```java
interface ExprVisitor<T> {
    T visit(Num n);
    T visit(Add a);
    T visit(Var v);
}

record Add(Expr left, Expr right) implements Expr {
    public <T> T accept(ExprVisitor<T> v) { return v.visit(this); }
}

class TypeCheckVisitor implements ExprVisitor<Class<?>> {
    public Class<?> visit(Add a) {
        if (a.left().accept(this) == Integer.class && a.right().accept(this) == Integer.class)
            return Integer.class;
        throw new RuntimeException("Type Error");
    }
    // ...
}
```

### 2. Flyweight Pattern for Terminals
**Optimization**: "A" and "True" might appear thousands of times in an AST.
**Implementation**: Cache `TerminalExpression` instances.
```java
class ExpressionFactory {
    static Map<String, VariableExpression> cache = new HashMap<>();
    public static VariableExpression get(String name) {
        return cache.computeIfAbsent(name, VariableExpression::new);
    }
}
```

### 3. JIT Compilation (The "Dragon Book" Approach)
**Optimization**: Instead of walking the tree every time, compile the AST into a `java.util.function.Predicate` or Bytecode.
```java
// Compile AST to a single Lambda
public Predicate<Context> compile(Expr e) {
    if (e instanceof And) {
        Predicate<Context> l = compile(((And)e).left);
        Predicate<Context> r = compile(((And)e).right);
        return ctx -> l.test(ctx) && r.test(ctx);
    }
    // ...
}
```
**Impact**: eliminates recursion overhead; runs at native speed.

### **Project 1: SQL Query Builder (The "Where" Clause)**
**Scenario**: You are building a secure ORM (like Hibernate or JOOQ) that needs to translate Java objects into SQL `WHERE` clauses.
**Why Interpreter?**: It allows you to build safe, compile-time checked queries without string concatenation (SQL Injection risk).

```java
import java.util.ArrayList;
import java.util.List;
import java.util.stream.Collectors;

// 1. Common Interface
interface SqlNode {
    String interpret();
}

// 2. Terminal Nodes (Columns, Values)
class Column implements SqlNode {
    private String name;
    public Column(String name) { this.name = name; }
    public String interpret() { return name; }
}

class StringValue implements SqlNode {
    private String val;
    public StringValue(String val) { this.val = val; }
    public String interpret() { return "'" + val.replace("'", "''") + "'"; } // Basic Sanitization
}

class IntValue implements SqlNode {
    private int val;
    public IntValue(int val) { this.val = val; }
    public String interpret() { return String.valueOf(val); }
}

// 3. Non-Terminal Nodes (Operators)
class Equals implements SqlNode {
    private SqlNode left, right;
    public Equals(SqlNode left, SqlNode right) { this.left = left; this.right = right; }
    public String interpret() { return left.interpret() + " = " + right.interpret(); }
}

class Or implements SqlNode {
    private SqlNode left, right;
    public Or(SqlNode left, SqlNode right) { this.left = left; this.right = right; }
    public String interpret() { return "(" + left.interpret() + " OR " + right.interpret() + ")"; }
}

class In implements SqlNode {
    private SqlNode col;
    private List<SqlNode> values;
    public In(SqlNode col, List<SqlNode> values) { this.col = col; this.values = values; }
    
    public String interpret() {
        String valStr = values.stream()
                .map(SqlNode::interpret)
                .collect(Collectors.joining(", "));
        return col.interpret() + " IN (" + valStr + ")";
    }
}

// 4. Client Usage
public class SqlBuilderDemo {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        // Query: name = 'Alice' OR (age IN (25, 30))
        
        SqlNode nameCol = new Column("name");
        SqlNode nameVal = new StringValue("Alice");
        SqlNode nameCheck = new Equals(nameCol, nameVal);
        
        SqlNode ageCol = new Column("age");
        List<SqlNode> ages = new ArrayList<>();
        ages.add(new IntValue(25));
        ages.add(new IntValue(30));
        SqlNode ageCheck = new In(ageCol, ages);
        
        SqlNode root = new Or(nameCheck, ageCheck);
        
        System.out.println("SQL: " + root.interpret()); 
        // Output: (name = 'Alice' OR age IN (25, 30))
    }
}
```

#### 🔍 Deep Dive: Why not just use Strings?
*   **Security**: The Interpreter enforces structure. You can add a `validate()` method to each node to prevent illegal column names.
*   ** composability**: You can pass `SqlNode` objects around. A "Filter Service" can return a `SqlNode` that you combine with another node. Strings don't compose safely.
