### **Project 2: Dynamic Fraud Detection Rule Engine**
**Scenario**: An e-commerce platform needs to flag transactions based on dynamic rules defined by risk analysts. Hardcoding these rules requires a deployment for every change. Ideally, rules are stored in a database string format.

**Key Requirements**:
1.  **Type Safety**: Handle Strings, Numbers, and Booleans.
2.  **Extensibility**: Add new operators (`IN`, `MATCHES`) easily.
3.  **Performance**: Evaluate millions of transactions per minute.

```java
import java.util.*;
import java.util.function.Predicate;

// 1. Context (The "Facts")
class TransactionContext {
    private Map<String, Object> facts = new HashMap<>();

    public void addFact(String key, Object value) {
        facts.put(key, value);
    }

    public Object getFact(String key) {
        if (!facts.containsKey(key)) {
            throw new IllegalArgumentException("Missing fact: " + key);
        }
        return facts.get(key);
    }
}

// 2. Abstract Expression
interface RuleExpression {
    boolean interpret(TransactionContext context);
}

// 3. Terminal Expressions
class FactCheck implements RuleExpression {
    private String factName;
    private Object expectedValue;

    public FactCheck(String factName, Object expectedValue) {
        this.factName = factName;
        this.expectedValue = expectedValue;
    }

    @Override
    public boolean interpret(TransactionContext context) {
        Object actual = context.getFact(factName);
        return expectedValue.equals(actual);
    }
}

class GreaterThan implements RuleExpression {
    private String factName;
    private double threshold;

    public GreaterThan(String factName, double threshold) {
        this.factName = factName;
        this.threshold = threshold;
    }

    @Override
    public boolean interpret(TransactionContext context) {
        Object val = context.getFact(factName);
        if (val instanceof Number) {
            return ((Number) val).doubleValue() > threshold;
        }
        return false; // Or throw TypeMismatchException
    }
}

// 4. Non-Terminal Expressions (Combinators)
class AndRule implements RuleExpression {
    private RuleExpression left, right;

    public AndRule(RuleExpression left, RuleExpression right) {
        this.left = left;
        this.right = right;
    }

    @Override
    public boolean interpret(TransactionContext context) {
        return left.interpret(context) && right.interpret(context);
    }
}

class OrRule implements RuleExpression {
    private RuleExpression left, right;

    public OrRule(RuleExpression left, RuleExpression right) {
        this.left = left;
        this.right = right;
    }

    @Override
    public boolean interpret(TransactionContext context) {
        return left.interpret(context) || right.interpret(context);
    }
}

// 5. Client / Parser (Builder)
public class FraudEngine {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        // Rule: (Amount > 10000) AND (Country == "HighRisk")
        RuleExpression highVal = new GreaterThan("amount", 10000);
        RuleExpression riskyCountry = new FactCheck("country", "HighRisk");
        RuleExpression fraudRule = new AndRule(highVal, riskyCountry);

        // Transaction 1: Legitimate
        TransactionContext t1 = new TransactionContext();
        t1.addFact("amount", 500.0);
        t1.addFact("country", "US");
        System.out.println("Transaction 1 Fraud: " + fraudRule.interpret(t1)); // false

        // Transaction 2: Fraudulent
        TransactionContext t2 = new TransactionContext();
        t2.addFact("amount", 15000.0);
        t2.addFact("country", "HighRisk");
        System.out.println("Transaction 2 Fraud: " + fraudRule.interpret(t2)); // true
    }
}
```

### **Project 3: Mathematical Expression Evaluator (Shunting Yard)**
**Scenario**: Building a scientific calculator or spreadsheet engine where users enter formulas like `3 + 5 * (10 - 2)`.
**Feature**: This implementation includes a **Parser** that converts Infix notation (Human readable) to the Interpreter's Tree structure.

```java
import java.util.*;

// --- The Interpreter Pattern ---
interface MathExpr {
    double interpret();
}

class Number implements MathExpr {
    private double n;
    public Number(double n) { this.n = n; }
    public double interpret() { return n; }
    @Override public String toString() { return String.valueOf(n); }
}

class Operation implements MathExpr {
    private MathExpr left, right;
    private char op;

    public Operation(MathExpr left, char op, MathExpr right) {
        this.left = left;
        this.op = op;
        this.right = right;
    }

    public double interpret() {
        double l = left.interpret();
        double r = right.interpret();
        return switch (op) {
            case '+' -> l + r;
            case '-' -> l - r;
            case '*' -> l * r;
            case '/' -> l / r; // Add div by zero check in prod
            default -> 0;
        };
    }
    @Override public String toString() { return "(" + left + " " + op + " " + right + ")"; }
}

// --- The Parser (Shunting Yard Algorithm) ---
// Note: This matches "Interpreter" with "Builder" effectively.
class ExpressionParser {
    public static MathExpr parse(String expression) {
        Stack<MathExpr> values = new Stack<>();
        Stack<Character> ops = new Stack<>();
        
        for (int i = 0; i < expression.length(); i++) {
            char c = expression.charAt(i);
            if (c == ' ') continue;
            
            if (Character.isDigit(c)) {
                StringBuilder sb = new StringBuilder();
                while (i < expression.length() && 
                       (Character.isDigit(expression.charAt(i)) || expression.charAt(i) == '.')) {
                    sb.append(expression.charAt(i++));
                }
                i--;
                values.push(new Number(Double.parseDouble(sb.toString())));
            } else if (c == '(') {
                ops.push(c);
            } else if (c == ')') {
                while (ops.peek() != '(') applyOp(ops.pop(), values);
                ops.pop();
            } else if (isOperator(c)) {
                while (!ops.isEmpty() && precedence(ops.peek()) >= precedence(c)) {
                    applyOp(ops.pop(), values);
                }
                ops.push(c);
            }
        }
        while (!ops.isEmpty()) applyOp(ops.pop(), values);
        return values.pop();
    }

    private static void applyOp(char op, Stack<MathExpr> values) {
        MathExpr right = values.pop();
        MathExpr left = values.pop();
        values.push(new Operation(left, op, right));
    }

    private static boolean isOperator(char c) {
        return c == '+' || c == '-' || c == '*' || c == '/';
    }

    private static int precedence(char op) {
        if (op == '+' || op == '-') return 1;
        if (op == '*' || op == '/') return 2;
        return 0;
    }
}

// Client
public class Calculator {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        String query = "10 + 2 * (15 - 5)";
        MathExpr ast = ExpressionParser.parse(query);
        System.out.println("AST: " + ast); // (10.0 + (2.0 * (15.0 - 5.0)))
        System.out.println("Result: " + ast.interpret()); // 30.0
    }
}
```

### **Project 4: Cron Expression Scheduler**
**Scenario**: You are building a Job Scheduler like Quartz or Kubernetes CronJob. You need to determine if a job should run at a specific second.
**Grammar**: `Minute Hour Day Month DayOfWeek` (e.g., `*/15 * * * *` = "Every 15 minutes").

```java
import java.time.LocalDateTime;

interface CronField {
    boolean matches(int value);
}

// 1. Terminal: Logic for "*" or "5" or "10-20"
class Always implements CronField { 
    public boolean matches(int value) { return true; } 
}

class Exact implements CronField {
    int val;
    public Exact(int val) { this.val = val; }
    public boolean matches(int value) { return this.val == value; }
}

class Range implements CronField {
    int start, end;
    public Range(int start, int end) { this.start = start; this.end = end; }
    public boolean matches(int value) { return value >= start && value <= end; }
}

class Step implements CronField { // "*/5"
    int step;
    public Step(int step) { this.step = step; }
    public boolean matches(int value) { return value % step == 0; }
}

// 2. Non-Terminal: The full expression
class CronExpression {
    CronField minute, hour, day, month, dow;

    public CronExpression(String expr) {
        // In a real interview, you'd write a parser here.
        // For now, hardcode "*/15 * * * *" logic:
        this.minute = new Step(15);
        this.hour = new Always();
        this.day = new Always();
        this.month = new Always();
        this.dow = new Always();
    }

    public boolean shouldRun(LocalDateTime now) {
        return minute.matches(now.getMinute()) &&
               hour.matches(now.getHour()) &&
               day.matches(now.getDayOfMonth()) &&
               month.matches(now.getMonthValue()) &&
               dow.matches(now.getDayOfWeek().getValue());
    }
}
```

### **Project 5: Mini-Regex Engine**
**Scenario**: Implementing a subset of Regex (`.` for any char, `*` for zero-or-more) to understand automata theory.
**Pattern**: Interpreting a pattern string against a text input.

```java
class RegexEngine {
    // 1. Dynamic Programming / Recursion Approach (Interpreter logic)
    public boolean isMatch(String s, String p) {
        if (p.isEmpty()) return s.isEmpty();

        boolean firstMatch = (!s.isEmpty() && 
                             (p.charAt(0) == s.charAt(0) || p.charAt(0) == '.'));

        if (p.length() >= 2 && p.charAt(1) == '*') {
            // Case 1: Treat '*' as 0 occurrences (skip pattern char and '*')
            // Case 2: Treat '*' as 1+ occurrences (consume char in s)
            return (isMatch(s, p.substring(2)) || 
                   (firstMatch && isMatch(s.substring(1), p)));
        } else {
            return firstMatch && isMatch(s.substring(1), p.substring(1));
        }
    }

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        RegexEngine re = new RegexEngine();
        System.out.println(re.isMatch("aa", "a*")); // true
        System.out.println(re.isMatch("ab", ".*")); // true
        System.out.println(re.isMatch("mississippi", "mis*is*p*.")); // false
    }
}
```
*Note: While implemented recursively here, a full Interpreter Pattern would convert the Regex pattern into an object graph (`Star(Dot())`) for reusability.*

### **Project 6: High-Frequency Trading Matcher (Bytecode Optimization)**
**Scenario**: Matching millions of orders per second. Standard object-based Intepreter is too slow (GC pauses).
**Solution**: "Compile" the rule into a `long[]` array of opcodes and interpret via a tight `switch` loop (Zero Garbage).

```java
// Simplified Bytecode Interpreter
public class IntMatcher {
    // OpCodes
    static final long LOAD_PRICE = 1;
    static final long LOAD_QTY = 2;
    static final long GT = 3; // >
    static final long LT = 4; // <
    static final long RET = 5; // Return boolean

    public static boolean match(long[] program, long price, long qty) {
        long reg = 0; // The "Accumulator" register
        
        for(int pc = 0; pc < program.length; pc++) {
            long op = program[pc];
            if (op == LOAD_PRICE) reg = price;
            else if (op == LOAD_QTY) reg = qty;
            else if (op == GT) {
                long val = program[++pc];
                if (reg <= val) return false;
            }
            else if (op == LT) {
                long val = program[++pc];
                if (reg >= val) return false;
            }
            else if (op == RET) return true;
        }
        return false;
    }

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        // Rule: Price > 100 AND Qty < 50
        // ASM: 
        // LOAD_PRICE
        // GT 100
        // LOAD_QTY
        // LT 50
        // RET
        long[] rule = {
            LOAD_PRICE, GT, 100,
            LOAD_QTY, LT, 50,
            RET
        };
        
        System.out.println(match(rule, 101, 40)); // true
        System.out.println(match(rule, 99, 40));  // false
    }
}
```
**Why Senior SDE?**: This shows you understand *how computers actually work*. It bridges the gap between Design Patterns and Computer Architecture.

### **Project 7: Smart Home Automation (Natural Language Processing)**
**Scenario**: Users want to control their smart home using natural language commands like "Turn on the lights in the kitchen" or "Set temperature to 72 degrees".
**Challenge**: Parsing natural language variants (`Turn on`, `Switch on`, `Enable`) and mapping them to actionable device commands.
**Solution**: A flexible Interpreter that builds a command object graph.

```java
import java.util.*;

// 1. Context - The State of the Home
class HomeContext {
    Map<String, Boolean> lights = new HashMap<>(); // room -> status
    Map<String, Integer> thermostats = new HashMap<>(); // room -> temp
    StringBuilder output = new StringBuilder();

    public void setLight(String room, boolean on) {
        lights.put(room.toLowerCase(), on);
        output.append("Light in ").append(room).append(" turned ").append(on ? "ON" : "OFF").append("\n");
    }

    public void setTemp(String room, int temp) {
        thermostats.put(room.toLowerCase(), temp);
        output.append("Thermostat in ").append(room).append(" set to ").append(temp).append("\n");
    }
    
    public String getLogs() { return output.toString(); }
}

// 2. Expressions
interface CommandExpression {
    void interpret(HomeContext ctx);
}

// Terminal: Action (Turn On / Set)
class ActionExpression implements CommandExpression {
    String action; // "on", "off", "set"
    public ActionExpression(String action) { this.action = action; }
    public void interpret(HomeContext ctx) { /* Context doesn't change here, just placeholder */ }
    public String getAction() { return action; }
}

// Terminal: Device/Target (Light/Thermostat)
class TargetExpression implements CommandExpression {
    String target; // "light", "thermostat"
    public TargetExpression(String target) { this.target = target; }
    public void interpret(HomeContext ctx) {}
    public String getTarget() { return target; }
}

// Terminal: Location (Kitchen, Living Room)
class LocationExpression implements CommandExpression {
    String location;
    public LocationExpression(String l) { this.location = l; }
    public void interpret(HomeContext ctx) {}
    public String getLocation() { return location; }
}

// Non-Terminal: Sentence (The fully parsed command)
class SentenceExpression implements CommandExpression {
    ActionExpression action;
    TargetExpression target;
    LocationExpression location;
    int value; // For temperature (optional)

    public SentenceExpression(ActionExpression a, TargetExpression t, LocationExpression l, int val) {
        this.action = a; this.target = t; this.location = l; this.value = val;
    }

    @Override
    public void interpret(HomeContext ctx) {
        String act = action.getAction();
        String tgt = target.getTarget();
        String loc = location.getLocation();

        if (tgt.equals("light")) {
            if (act.equals("on")) ctx.setLight(loc, true);
            else if (act.equals("off")) ctx.setLight(loc, false);
        } else if (tgt.equals("thermostat")) {
            if (act.equals("set")) ctx.setTemp(loc, value);
        }
    }
}

// 3. Parser (Simple NLP)
class SmartHomeParser {
    public static CommandExpression parse(String command) {
        // "Turn on light in Kitchen"
        // "Set thermostat to 72 in Bedroom"
        String[] tokens = command.toLowerCase().split(" ");
        String actionStr = "";
        String targetStr = "";
        String locationStr = "";
        int val = 0;

        for (int i = 0; i < tokens.length; i++) {
            if (tokens[i].equals("turn") && i+1 < tokens.length) {
                if (tokens[i+1].equals("on")) actionStr = "on";
                if (tokens[i+1].equals("off")) actionStr = "off";
            }
            if (tokens[i].equals("set")) actionStr = "set";
            
            if (tokens[i].equals("light") || tokens[i].equals("lights")) targetStr = "light";
            if (tokens[i].equals("thermostat") || tokens[i].equals("temperature")) targetStr = "thermostat";
            
            if (tokens[i].equals("kitchen")) locationStr = "kitchen";
            if (tokens[i].equals("bedroom")) locationStr = "bedroom";
            if (tokens[i].equals("living") && i+1 < tokens.length && tokens[i+1].equals("room")) locationStr = "living room";

            if (Character.isDigit(tokens[i].charAt(0))) val = Integer.parseInt(tokens[i]);
        }
        
        return new SentenceExpression(
            new ActionExpression(actionStr),
            new TargetExpression(targetStr),
            new LocationExpression(locationStr),
            val
        );
    }
}

// 4. Client
public class SmartHomeDemo {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        HomeContext home = new HomeContext();
        String cmd1 = "Turn on lights in Kitchen";
        String cmd2 = "Set thermostat to 72 in Living Room";
        
        SmartHomeParser.parse(cmd1).interpret(home);
        SmartHomeParser.parse(cmd2).interpret(home);
        
        System.out.print(home.getLogs());
        /* Output:
           Light in kitchen turned ON
           Thermostat in living room set to 72
        */
    }
}
```
**Key Takeaway**: The Interpreter pattern allows you to decouple the *grammar* (how users speak) from the *execution* (API calls). You can extend the parser to support "Dim lights to 50%" without changing the `HomeContext`.

### **Project 8: Functional Reactive Stream (RxJava Clone)**
**Scenario**: You are building a streaming data library. You need to allow users to chain operations like `filter`, `map`, and `reduce`.
**Pattern**: Each operator is a Non-Terminal Expression that interprets a stream of data.

```java
import java.util.ArrayList;
import java.util.List;
import java.util.function.Function;
import java.util.function.Predicate;

// 1. The Stream Expression (Interpreter Interface)
interface StreamExpr<T> {
    List<T> evaluate();
}

// 2. Terminal: Source (The raw data)
class Source<T> implements StreamExpr<T> {
    private List<T> data;
    public Source(List<T> data) { this.data = data; }
    public List<T> evaluate() { return new ArrayList<>(data); }
}

// 3. Non-Terminal: Filter
class Filter<T> implements StreamExpr<T> {
    private StreamExpr<T> input;
    private Predicate<T> predicate;
    
    public Filter(StreamExpr<T> input, Predicate<T> p) {
        this.input = input;
        this.predicate = p;
    }
    
    public List<T> evaluate() {
        List<T> result = new ArrayList<>();
        for (T item : input.evaluate()) {
            if (predicate.test(item)) result.add(item);
        }
        return result;
    }
}

// 4. Non-Terminal: Map
class MapOp<T, R> implements StreamExpr<R> {
    private StreamExpr<T> input;
    private Function<T, R> mapper;
    
    public MapOp(StreamExpr<T> input, Function<T, R> m) {
        this.input = input;
        this.mapper = m;
    }
    
    public List<R> evaluate() {
        List<R> result = new ArrayList<>();
        for (T item : input.evaluate()) {
            result.add(mapper.apply(item));
        }
        return result;
    }
}

// 5. Fluent API Wrapper (Builder + Interpreter)
class FluentStream<T> {
    private StreamExpr<T> expr;
    
    private FluentStream(StreamExpr<T> expr) { this.expr = expr; }
    
    public static <T> FluentStream<T> of(List<T> data) {
        return new FluentStream<>(new Source<>(data));
    }
    
    public FluentStream<T> filter(Predicate<T> p) {
        return new FluentStream<>(new Filter<>(this.expr, p));
    }
    
    public <R> FluentStream<R> map(Function<T, R> m) {
        return new FluentStream<>(new MapOp<>(this.expr, m));
    }
    
    public List<T> toList() {
        return expr.evaluate(); // The Interpreter runs here!
    }
}

// 6. Client
public class ReactiveDemo {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        List<String> rawData = List.of("apple", "banana", "avocado", "cherry");
        
        // Interpreted chain:
        // MapOp(Filter(Source, startsWith 'a'), toUpperCase)
        List<String> result = FluentStream.of(rawData)
            .filter(s -> s.startsWith("a"))
            .map(String::toUpperCase)
            .toList();
            
        System.out.println(result); // [APPLE, AVOCADO]
    }
}
```
**Why Interpreter?**: It builds a lazy evaluation tree. The data doesn't flow until `toList()` (terminal operation) is called. This mimics Java Streams or RxJava.

### **Project 9: Musical Notation Sequencer (MIDI)**
**Scenario**: A music composition software where specific symbols denote note duration, pitch, and repetition.
**Grammar**: `C4 q` (C note, octave 4, quarter), `D4 h` (D note, half), `[ E4 q ] x2` (Repeat block).

```java
import java.util.*;

// 1. Context (The Playback Engine)
class MusicContext {
    private int bpm = 120;
    private StringBuilder track = new StringBuilder();
    
    public void playNote(String note, int octave, double duration) {
        double durationMs = (60000.0 / bpm) * duration;
        track.append(String.format("PLAY %s%d for %.0fms\n", note, octave, durationMs));
    }
    public void setBpm(int bpm) { this.bpm = bpm; }
    public String getTrack() { return track.toString(); }
}

// 2. Expression
interface MusicExpr {
    void play(MusicContext ctx);
}

// 3. Terminal: Note
class Note implements MusicExpr {
    String key;     // C, D, E
    int octave;     // 4, 5
    String len;     // q=1.0, h=2.0, w=4.0
    
    public Note(String key, int octave, String len) {
        this.key = key; this.octave = octave; this.len = len;
    }
    
    public void play(MusicContext ctx) {
        double duration = switch(len) {
            case "w" -> 4.0;
            case "h" -> 2.0;
            case "q" -> 1.0;
            case "e" -> 0.5;
            default -> 1.0;
        };
        ctx.playNote(key, octave, duration);
    }
}

// 4. Non-Terminal: Measure (Sequence of Notes)
class Measure implements MusicExpr {
    List<MusicExpr> notes = new ArrayList<>();
    public void add(MusicExpr n) { notes.add(n); }
    
    public void play(MusicContext ctx) {
        for (MusicExpr n : notes) n.play(ctx);
    }
}

// 5. Non-Terminal: Repeat (Loop)
class Repeat implements MusicExpr {
    MusicExpr loopBody;
    int count;
    
    public Repeat(MusicExpr body, int count) {
        this.loopBody = body;
        this.count = count;
    }
    
    public void play(MusicContext ctx) {
        for (int i = 0; i < count; i++) {
            loopBody.play(ctx);
        }
    }
}

// 6. Client
public class MusicDemo {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        MusicContext synth = new MusicContext();
        synth.setBpm(100);
        
        // Melody: C4(q) D4(q) then [E4(h)] x 2
        Measure mainTheme = new Measure();
        mainTheme.add(new Note("C", 4, "q"));
        mainTheme.add(new Note("D", 4, "q"));
        
        Measure chorus = new Measure();
        chorus.add(new Note("E", 4, "h"));
        
        mainTheme.add(new Repeat(chorus, 2)); // Repeat E4 twice
        
        mainTheme.play(synth);
        
        System.out.println(synth.getTrack());
        /* Output:
           PLAY C4 for 600ms
           PLAY D4 for 600ms
           PLAY E4 for 1200ms
           PLAY E4 for 1200ms
        */
    }
}
```
**Optimization**: In a real synth, `playNote` would send MIDI byte signals. The Interpreter ensures the *structure* of the song (repeats, tempos) is abstract and manipulatable.

### **Project 10: Text Adventure Game Engine (Interactive Fiction)**
**Scenario**: Creating a game where players type commands like "Go North", "Take Sword", "Use Key on Door".
**Pattern**: Interpreting Verb-Noun or Verb-Noun-Preposition-Noun structures.

```java
import java.util.*;

// 1. Context
class GameContext {
    String currentRoom = "Entrance";
    List<String> inventory = new ArrayList<>();
    Map<String, String> roomDescriptions = new HashMap<>();
    
    public GameContext() {
        roomDescriptions.put("Entrance", "You are in a dark hall. Exits: North.");
        roomDescriptions.put("Hallway", "A long corridor. Exits: South, East.");
        roomDescriptions.put("Kitchen", "Smells like burning toast. Exits: West.");
    }
    
    public void move(String direction) {
        if (currentRoom.equals("Entrance") && direction.equalsIgnoreCase("north")) currentRoom = "Hallway";
        elif (currentRoom.equals("Hallway") && direction.equalsIgnoreCase("south")) currentRoom = "Entrance";
        elif (currentRoom.equals("Hallway") && direction.equalsIgnoreCase("east")) currentRoom = "Kitchen";
        elif (currentRoom.equals("Kitchen") && direction.equalsIgnoreCase("west")) currentRoom = "Hallway";
        else System.out.println("You can't go that way.");
    }
    
    public void take(String item) {
        inventory.add(item);
        System.out.println("Taken: " + item);
    }
    
    public void look() {
        System.out.println(roomDescriptions.getOrDefault(currentRoom, "Unknown Void"));
    }
}

// 2. Expressions
interface GameCommand {
    void execute(GameContext ctx);
}

class MoveCommand implements GameCommand {
    String direction;
    public MoveCommand(String d) { this.direction = d; }
    public void execute(GameContext ctx) { ctx.move(direction); }
}

class TakeCommand implements GameCommand {
    String item;
    public TakeCommand(String i) { this.item = i; }
    public void execute(GameContext ctx) { ctx.take(item); }
}

class LookCommand implements GameCommand {
    public void execute(GameContext ctx) { ctx.look(); }
}

// 3. Parser
class CommandParser {
    public static GameCommand parse(String input) {
        String[] parts = input.trim().split(" ");
        String verb = parts[0].toLowerCase();
        
        if (verb.equals("go") && parts.length > 1) return new MoveCommand(parts[1]);
        if (verb.equals("take") && parts.length > 1) return new TakeCommand(parts[1]);
        if (verb.equals("look")) return new LookCommand();
        
        return ctx -> System.out.println("I don't understand.");
    }
}

// 4. Client
public class AdventureDemo {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        GameContext game = new GameContext();
        Scanner scanner = new Scanner(System.in);
        
        // Simulation of user input
        List<String> inputs = List.of("Look", "Go North", "Look", "Go East", "Take Apple");
        
        for (String in : inputs) {
            System.out.println("> " + in);
            CommandParser.parse(in).execute(game);
        }
    }
}
```

### **Project 11: L-System Fractal Generator (Turtle Graphics)**
**Scenario**: Generating complex organic shapes (plants, trees) using a simple string rewriting rule set (Lindenmayer System) and a Logo-style Turtle interpreter.
**Grammar**: `F` (Move Forward), `+` (Turn Right), `-` (Turn Left), `[` (Save State), `]` (Restore State).

```java
import java.util.*;

// 1. Context (The Turtle)
class Turtle {
    double x = 0, y = 0;
    double angle = 90; // Up
    Stack<Double[]> stack = new Stack<>();
    
    public void forward(double dist) {
        double rad = Math.toRadians(angle);
        double dx = Math.cos(rad) * dist;
        double dy = Math.sin(rad) * dist;
        System.out.printf("Line from (%.2f, %.2f) to (%.2f, %.2f)\n", x, y, x+dx, y+dy);
        x += dx; y += dy;
    }
    
    public void turn(double deg) { angle -= deg; }
    
    public void push() { stack.push(new Double[]{x, y, angle}); }
    
    public void pop() {
        Double[] state = stack.pop();
        x = state[0]; y = state[1]; angle = state[2];
    }
}

// 2. Expressions
interface LExpr {
    void interpret(Turtle t);
}

class Forward implements LExpr {
    public void interpret(Turtle t) { t.forward(10); }
}

class TurnRight implements LExpr {
    public void interpret(Turtle t) { t.turn(-25); } // Turn right 25 deg
}

class TurnLeft implements LExpr {
    public void interpret(Turtle t) { t.turn(25); }
}

class Save implements LExpr {
    public void interpret(Turtle t) { t.push(); }
}

class Restore implements LExpr {
    public void interpret(Turtle t) { t.pop(); }
}

// 3. Parser / Compiler
class LSystem {
    public static List<LExpr> parse(String instruction) {
        List<LExpr> list = new ArrayList<>();
        for (char c : instruction.toCharArray()) {
            switch(c) {
                case 'F': list.add(new Forward()); break;
                case '+': list.add(new TurnRight()); break;
                case '-': list.add(new TurnLeft()); break;
                case '[': list.add(new Save()); break;
                case ']': list.add(new Restore()); break;
            }
        }
        return list;
    }
    
    // Expand rules: F -> F[+F]F[-F]F
    public static String expand(String axiom, int iterations) {
        String current = axiom;
        for(int i=0; i<iterations; i++) {
            StringBuilder next = new StringBuilder();
            for(char c : current.toCharArray()) {
                if(c == 'F') next.append("F[+F]F[-F]F"); // Tree Rule
                else next.append(c);
            }
            current = next.toString();
        }
        return current;
    }
}

// 4. Client
public class FractalDemo {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        String axiom = "F";
        String tree = LSystem.expand(axiom, 2); // Generate string
        System.out.println("Fractal String: " + tree);
        
        List<LExpr> program = LSystem.parse(tree); // Compile to AST
        
        Turtle turtle = new Turtle();
        for (LExpr expr : program) {
            expr.interpret(turtle);
        }
    }
}
```
**Why Senior SDE?**: This demonstrates knowledge of **Computer Graphics**, **State Management** (Stack), and **Generative Algorithms**, all wrapped in the Interpreter Pattern.

### **Project 12: Performance Benchmarking (JMH)**
**Scenario**: You need to prove to your manager that the Interpreter pattern is fast enough (or when to optimize).
**Tool**: Java Microbenchmark Harness (JMH).

```java
import org.openjdk.jmh.annotations.*;
import java.util.concurrent.TimeUnit;

@State(Scope.Thread)
@BenchmarkMode(Mode.AverageTime)
@OutputTimeUnit(TimeUnit.NANOSECONDS)
public class InterpreterBenchmark {

    private int a = 10, b = 20;
    
    // 1. Hardcoded Java (Baseline)
    @Benchmark
    public int hardcoded() {
        return (a + b) * (a - b);
    }
    
    // 2. Interpreter Pattern
    Expression expr;
    Context ctx;
    
    @Setup
    public void setup() {
        ctx = new Context();
        ctx.set("a", 10);
        ctx.set("b", 20);
        // (a + b) * (a - b)
        expr = new Mult(
            new Add(new Var("a"), new Var("b")),
            new Sub(new Var("a"), new Var("b"))
        );
    }
    
    @Benchmark
    public int interpreter() {
        return expr.interpret(ctx);
    }
    
    // 3. Lambda (Compiled Style)
    java.util.function.ToIntFunction<Context> lambda;
    
    @Setup
    public void setupLambda() {
        int l_a = 10, l_b = 20;
         lambda = (c) -> (c.get("a") + c.get("b")) * (c.get("a") - c.get("b"));
    }
    
    @Benchmark
    public int lambda() {
        return lambda.applyAsInt(ctx);
    }
}
/*
 * RESULTS (Approximate):
 * Hardcoded:   2.1 ns/op  (CPU Register math)
 * Lambda:      5.4 ns/op  (Method call overhead)
 * Interpreter: 45.0 ns/op (Pointer chasing, virtual calls)
 *
 * CONCLUSION: Interpreter is ~20x slower than raw Java. 
 * Use it for FLEXIBILITY, not for tight loops in HFT systems.
 */
```

### **13. Deep Dive: Security Vulnerabilities & Mitigations**

#### **1. ReDoS (Regular Expression Denial of Service)**
**The Threat**: The Interpreter Pattern is often used to implement Regex-like engines. If implemented naively using Backtracking, it is vulnerable to **Catastrophic Backtracking**.
*   **Input**: `(a+)+` matches `aaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaa!`
*   **Complexity**: $O(2^N)$
*   **Result**: The server hangs for years evaluating a 30-char string.

**Code Example (Vulnerable)**:
```java
class Repeat implements RegexNode {
    // Naively tries all possibilities
    public boolean match(String input) {
        // ... backtracking logic ...
    }
}
```

**Mitigation**:
1.  **Thompson's Construction**: Convert the AST to an NFA (Nondeterministic Finite Automaton) and then run it. This guarantees $O(N)$ performance.
2.  **Timeout**: Enforce a strict millisecond timeout for any `interpret()` call.
3.  **Depth Limit**: Reject expressions with nesting depth > 10.

#### **2. Stack Overflow Attacks**
**The Threat**: Since the Interpreter Pattern relies heavily on recursion (`interpret` calls `interpret`), a malicious user can craft a payload that is extremely deep.
*   **Payload**: `((((....1+1....))))` (10,000 layers deep)
*   **Result**: `JVM StackOverflowError`, crashing the thread or application.

**Mitigation**:
*   **Trampolining**: Convert the recursion into a loop using a `Stack` data structure on the Heap.
*   **Depth Counter**:
```java
public Object interpret(Context ctx, int depth) {
    if (depth > 500) throw new SecurityException("Expression Limit Exceeded");
    return left.interpret(ctx, depth + 1) + right.interpret(ctx, depth + 1);
}
```

#### **3. Cycle Detection**
**The Threat**: In spreadsheet-like environments (e.g., Project 3), users can define circular references.
*   `A = B + 1`
*   `B = A + 1`
*   **Result**: Infinite Recursion.

**Mitigation**:
*   Pass a `Set<String> visited` context down the call stack.
*   **Before** evaluating a variable, check if it's in `visited`.
*   **After** evaluating, remove it from `visited`.

---

### **14. Multi-Language Perspectives**

#### **Python Perspective: The Power of `ast` and `eval`**
Python's dynamic nature makes it an Interpreter playground.
1.  **`eval()` / `exec()`**: The built-in interpreter. *Dangerous* but powerful.
2.  **`ast` module**: Python exposes its own AST parser. You can modify it at runtime (Metaprogramming).

```python
import ast
import operator

# Safe Math Interpreter using Python's own AST
ops = {ast.Add: operator.add, ast.Sub: operator.sub}

def eval_expr(expr):
    node = ast.parse(expr, mode='eval')
    
    def _eval(node):
        if isinstance(node, ast.Expression):
            return _eval(node.body)
        elif isinstance(node, ast.Constant): # <number>
            return node.value
        elif isinstance(node, ast.BinOp):    # <left> <op> <right>
            return ops[type(node.op)](_eval(node.left), _eval(node.right))
        raise TypeError(node)

    return _eval(node)

print(eval_expr("1 + 5 - 2")) # 4
```

#### **C++ Perspective: Template Metaprogramming (Compile-Time Interpreter)**
In C++, you can write an Interpreter that runs **during compilation**.
*   **Expression Templates**: Used by libraries like Eigen (Linear Algebra) to optimize `Vector A = B + C * D` into a single loop, avoiding temporary objects.
*   **Constexpr**: Modern C++ allows executing complex logic at compile time.

```cpp
template<int N>
struct Factorial {
    static const int value = N * Factorial<N - 1>::value;
};

template<>
struct Factorial<0> {
    static const int value = 1;
};

// Calculated by the compiler. Run-time cost is zero (literally a constant).
int main() {
    int x = Factorial<5>::value; // 120
}
```

#### **Go Perspective: Interfaces and Type Switches**
Go lacks inheritance, so the Interpreter pattern relies on **Interfaces**.
The standard library `text/template` is a prime example of a robust, secure Interpreter.

```go
type Node interface {
    Eval(ctx context.Context) (interface{}, error)
}

// Uses Type Switches instead of Polymorphism sometimes
func (n *AddNode) Eval(ctx context.Context) (interface{}, error) {
    l, _ := n.Left.Eval(ctx)
    r, _ := n.Right.Eval(ctx)
    return l.(int) + r.(int), nil
}
```

### **15. Interview Defense: "Why Interpreter?"**

| Question | Strong Answer (Senior SDE) |
| :--- | :--- |
| **"Why not use a Visitor?"** | "Visitor is for *extending functionality* (e.g., adding type checking) without changing classes. Interpreter is for *defining the grammar*. I often use them together: Interpreter defines the structure, Visitor executes it." |
| **"Is it slow?"** | "Yes, AST traversal is slow due to pointer chasing and virtual calls. If performance is critical, I would compile the AST to Bytecode (ASM) or use the **Flyweight Pattern** to cache terminal nodes." |
| **"When to avoid?"** | "Don't use it for complex languages (Java/C++). It's for simple DSLs. If grammar has 100+ rules, use a parser generator like ANTLR or JavaCC." |
| **"How to secure it?"** | "Strict stack depth limits, timeouts, and removing 'Turing Completeness' (no loops) if not needed." |

---
### **The Ultimate Interpreter Cheatsheet**

#### 1. Architecture Diagram (ASCII)

```plaintext
       Client
         |
         v
    [ Context ] <-------+
         |              |
         v              |
   [ Abstract ] <-------+----------------+
  [ Expression ]                         |
         ^                               |
         | (implements)                  | (implements)
  +------+------+               +--------+--------+
  |             |               |                 |
[ Terminal ] [ Terminal ]   [ NonTerminal ] [ NonTerminal ]
(Number)     (Variable)     (Add)           (Loop)
                               |     \           |
                             [Expr]  [Expr]    [Expr]
```

#### 2. Decision Matrix: When to use?

| Criteria | **Interpreter Pattern** | **Hardcoded / Recursive Descent** | **Compiler / Bytecode** |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Grammar Complexity** | Simple (L-System, Regex-lite) | Medium (JSON, basic math) | High (Java, C++) |
| **Performance** | Slow (Object overhead) | Medium | Fast (Native) |
| **Flexibility** | High (Change rules at runtime) | Low (Recompile needed) | Low (Recompile needed) |
| **Implementation Effort** | Medium | Medium | High |
| **Memory Usage** | High (Many objects) | Low (Stack based) | Low (Flat array) |

#### 3. Pattern Implementation Checklist

| Component | Essential? | Purpose |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **AbstractExpression** | ✅ Yes | Defines the `interpret(Context)` contract. |
| **TerminalExpression** | ✅ Yes | Leaf nodes (Literals, Variables). Returns data. |
| **NonTerminalExpression** | ✅ Yes | Composite nodes (Operators). Recursively calls children. |
| **Context** | ✅ Yes | Global state (Variables, Input Stream, Game World). |
| **Client** | ✅ Yes | Parses the string into the AST and calls `interpret()`. |
| **Visitor (Optional)** | ❌ No | Adds operations like PrettyPrint, TypeCheck without changing AST. |
| **Flyweight (Optional)** | ❌ No | Caches Terminal expressions to save memory. |

#### 4. Common Pitfalls & Fixes

*   **Pitfall**: **Class Explosion**. Creating a class for every tiny rule (`Add`, `Sub`, `Mult`, `Div`...).
    *   *Fix*: Use Enums or Lambdas for simple operations (`BinaryOp(TokenType.PLUS)`).
*   **Pitfall**: **Stack Overflow**. Deeply nested expressions crash the JVM.
    *   *Fix*: Limit recursion depth or switch to a Stack-based Iterative approach.
*   **Pitfall**: **Performance Bottlenecks**.
    *   *Fix*: Implement the **Visitor Pattern** to "compile" the AST into a faster format before execution.
*   **Pitfall**: **Coupling**. The Interpreter logic is mixed with the Data logic.
    *   *Fix*: Keep `Context` separate. Pass it as an argument, don't store it in the Node.

#### 5. Quick mental model
> "The Interpreter Pattern is just the **Composite Pattern** with a specific method: `interpret(Context)`."

### **SECTION 10: INTERVIEW DEFENSE & FAQ**

#### 🧠 Tough Questions from FAANG Interviewers

**Q1: The Interpreter Pattern is slow due to object overhead. How do you fix this?**
*   **Answer**: "That's correct. Each node is an object, leading to pointer chasing and cache misses. In a production system like a high-frequency trading rule engine, I would:
    1.  **Flyweight Pattern**: Deduplicate terminal nodes (e.g., share the '5' object).
    2.  **Compilation**: Instead of interpreting the tree every time, traverse it *once* to generate a Java `Predicate<Context>` or even emit Bytecode (using ASM) for near-native speed. This turns the 'Interpreter' into a 'Compiler'."

**Q2: How do you handle circular references in your expression?**
*   **Answer**: "In a pure tree, cycles aren't possible. However, if we allow 'variables' that reference other expressions (like in Excel), cycles can occur. I would implement **Cycle Detection** using a `visited` set within the Context or during the parsing phase (Topological Sort). If a node sees itself in the current recursion stack, throw a `CircularDependencyException`."

**Q3: What if the grammar becomes too complex for manual classes?**
*   **Answer**: "If the grammar approaches a full programming language (loops, functions), manual Interpreter classes become unmanageable. At that point, I would switch to a parser generator like ANTLR or JavaCC to generate the AST, and potentially use the **Visitor Pattern** to separate the logic (evaluation vs. type checking) from the nodes."

**Q4: Compare Interpreter vs. Visitor Pattern.**
*   **Answer**:
    *   **Interpreter**: Logic is *inside* the nodes (`interpret()` method). Good when the grammar is stable but you want to mix-and-match expressions.
    *   **Visitor**: Logic is *outside* the nodes (in a `Visitor` class). Good when the grammar is stable but you want to differ operations (Eval, Print, Save, Analyze) without changing the node classes.
    *   *Senior Tip*: "In reality, they are often used together. The structure is the Interpreter (AST), and the execution logic is a Visitor."

#### Q77: How does Double Dispatch differ from Method Overloading?
**Companies**: Microsoft (Game Engines), Amazon (Rule Engines), Adobe (Graphics Hit-Testing)
**Difficulty**: **Hard** (Polymorphism / Language Features)
**Category**: Behavioral Patterns, Type System

---

### **1. Conceptual Overview & Motivation**
#### **The "Why": Interaction Between Two Unknowns**
Imagine you are building a **Game Engine** or a **UI Framework**. You have a generic collision method:
`void collide(GameObject a, GameObject b)`

**The Challenge**:
*   If **Asteroid** hits **Ship** -> Ship takes damage.
*   If **Asteroid** hits **Asteroid** -> Both bounce.
*   If **Missile** hits **Asteroid** -> Asteroid explodes.

**The Problem**: Single Dispatch (Java/C++/Python).
When you call `a.collide(b)`:
1.  Runtime decides which class `a` is (Dynamic Dispatch).
2.  But `b` is treated as the *compile-time* type (usually `GameObject`).
3.  You end up in a generic `collide(GameObject)` method, losing the specific type of `b`.

**The Solution**: Double Dispatch.
We need **two rounds** of polymorphism to resolve two unknown types.
1.  **Round 1**: `a.collide(b)` -> Decides `a` is `Asteroid`.
2.  **Round 2**: Inside `Asteroid`, call `b.collideWith(this)` -> Decides `b` is `Ship`.

Now we are in `Ship.collideWith(Asteroid)`, where we know the **exact types of BOTH objects**.

#### **Visualization: The Interactive Dispatch Matrix**
Before diving into code, understand the flow with this interactive matrix:
[**🔴 View Double Dispatch Visualization**](./vis/double_dispatch_viz.html)

---

### **2. Solution Progression - Brute Force to Optimal**

#### **Approach 1: `instanceof` Chain (Brute Force)**
The naive approach is to use a massive `if-else` chain to manualy check types.

```java
// ❌ BAD: The "God Method" Anti-Pattern
class CollisionManager {
    public void collide(GameObject a, GameObject b) {
        if (a instanceof Asteroid && b instanceof Ship) {
            ((Ship)b).takeDamage(10);
        } else if (a instanceof Asteroid && b instanceof Missile) {
            ((Asteroid)a).destroy();
        } else if (a instanceof Ship && b instanceof Asteroid) {
            ((Ship)a).takeDamage(10);
        }
        // ... hundreds of combinations ...
    }
}
```

**Critique**:
*   **O(N) Checks**: Linear scan of types is slow.
*   **Violates OCP**: Adding a `UFO` class requires modifying this central file.
*   **Type Safety**: Manual casting `(Ship)b` is prone to errors.

#### **Approach 2: Method Overloading (The Static Trap)**
Many developers try to use Java's overloading:

```java
// ❌ WRONG: Java Overloading is STATIC
class Asteroid {
    void collide(Ship s) { ... }    // Specific
    void collide(Missile m) { ... } // Specific
    void collide(GameObject g) { ... } // Generic
}

GameObject a = new Asteroid();
GameObject b = new Ship();
a.collide(b); // CALLS collide(GameObject), NOT collide(Ship)!
```

**The Trap**: Overloading is determined at **Compile Time** based on the variable type (`GameObject`), not the runtime object.

#### **Approach 3: The Visitor Pattern (Optimal)**
This utilizes **Double Virtual Dispatch** to route execution to the correct handler.

```java
// ✅ OPTIMAL: Visitor Pattern
interface GameObject {
    void collide(GameObject other);          // Entry Point
    void collideWith(Asteroid asteroid);     // Handler 1
    void collideWith(Ship ship);             // Handler 2
}

class Asteroid implements GameObject {
    // 1. First Dispatch: Resolves 'this' is Asteroid
    public void collide(GameObject other) {
        other.collideWith(this); 
        // 2. Second Dispatch: Calls other's specific method for Asteroid
    }

    public void collideWith(Asteroid a) { /* Bounce */ }
    public void collideWith(Ship s) { /* Destruction */ }
}
```

---

### **3. Multi-Language Implementations**

#### **Java Implementation (Visitor)**
```java
public interface Unit {
    void interact(Unit other);
    void interactWith(Tank tank);
    void interactWith(Soldier soldier);
}
// See Project 4 for full implementation
```

#### **Python Implementation (`functools.singledispatch`)**
Python doesn't have native double dispatch, but the standard library offers a decorator for single dispatch based on type.

```python
from functools import singledispatch

@singledispatch
def collide(a, b):
    print("Generic collision")

@collide.register(Asteroid)
def _(a, b):
    # We know 'a' is Asteroid. Now dispatch on 'b'.
    collide_asteroid(b, a)
```

#### **C++ Implementation (Virtual Functions)**
C++ works exactly like Java (Single Dispatch). You must use `virtual` functions for the Visitor pattern.
However, `dynamic_cast` can be used for a slightly slower but more flexible Approach 1.

#### **Julia / C# (Native Support)**
**Julia** supports Multiple Dispatch natively.
```julia
collide(a::Asteroid, s::Ship) = println("Boom")
# The compiler picks the most specific method automatically.
```

---

### **4. Edge Cases & Error Handling**

1.  **Null Arguments**:
    *   If `other` is null in `other.collideWith(this)`, you get an immediate NPE.
    *   **Fix**: Add `@NotNull` checks.

2.  **Inheritance Depth**:
    *   If `MegaAsteroid extends Asteroid` and doesn't override `collideWith`, it inherits `Asteroid`'s behavior.
    *   **Risk**: If logic relies on exact types, this might be incorrect.

3.  **The "Expression Problem"**:
    *   Adding a NEW Type (`UFO`) requires modifying the Interface and ALL existing classes to add `collideWith(UFO)`.
    *   **Mitigation**: Default methods in interface (Java 8+) can provide a fallback, avoiding breaking changes.

---

### **5. Interview Simulation & Communication**

#### **The "Whiteboard" Strategy**
1.  **Draw the Grid**: Draw a 2x2 matrix (Asteroid/Ship vs Asteroid/Ship).
2.  **Show the Fail**: Write `a.collide(b)` and ask the interviewer "Which method is called?". Explain Static Dispatch.
3.  **Derive the Fix**: "We need to tell `b` what `a` is. Let's pass `this`."

#### **Defending the Design**
*   **Interviewer**: "Why not just use `instanceof`? It's cleaner than 20 methods."
*   **You**: "Performance and OCP. `instanceof` is linear O(N). Virtual calls are constant O(1). Also, the Visitor pattern forces me to handle all cases; `if-else` chains can miss one silently."

---

### **6. Advanced Optimizations**

#### **Optimization 1: The Collision Matrix (Hash Map)**
For systems with hundreds of types, the Visitor pattern bloats classes.
**Alternative**: A `Map<Pair<Class, Class>, Handler>`.
*   **Pros**: Decoupled logic.
*   **Cons**: Hash lookup overhead vs V-Table.

#### **Optimization 2: V-Table Performance**
A Virtual Call allows the CPU to use Branch Prediction.
Double Dispatch = 2 Virtual Calls + 2 Branch Predictions.
This is significantly faster than `if (type == A) ... else if (type == B) ...` which trashes the instruction pipeline.

---

### **7. Related Problems & Patterns**
1.  **Visitor Pattern**: The formal GoF name for Double Dispatch. Used in compilers (AST traversal).
2.  **Strategy Pattern**: Can be used to plug in different collision behaviors.
3.  **Mediator Pattern**: A central `CollisionMediator` can replace the distributed dispatch logic.

### **8. Production System Integration (THE PROJECTS)**

#### **Project 1: Enterprise Event Bus (UI Framework)**
**Scenario**: A robust UI framework where specific Components handle specific Events differently.
*   `Button` + `ClickEvent` -> Fire Action.
*   `Window` + `ClickEvent` -> Bring to Front.
*   `Window` + `ScrollEvent` -> Scroll Content.
*   `Panel` + `DragEvent` -> Move Panel.
*   `TextField` + `KeyEvent` -> Input Text.

**Implementation**:
```java
// 1. THE EVENTS HIERARCHY
interface UIEvent {
    void dispatch(UIComponent component);
    long getTimestamp();
    int getSourceId();
}

abstract class BaseEvent implements UIEvent {
    private final long timestamp = System.currentTimeMillis();
    private final int sourceId;
    public BaseEvent(int id) { this.sourceId = id; }
    public long getTimestamp() { return timestamp; }
    public int getSourceId() { return sourceId; }
}

class ClickEvent extends BaseEvent {
    public ClickEvent(int id) { super(id); }
    public void dispatch(UIComponent c) { c.handle(this); }
    public String toString() { return "Click@" + getTimestamp(); }
}

class ScrollEvent extends BaseEvent {
    public final int deltaY;
    public ScrollEvent(int id, int dy) { super(id); this.deltaY = dy; }
    public void dispatch(UIComponent c) { c.handle(this); }
}

class DragEvent extends BaseEvent {
    public final int x, y;
    public DragEvent(int id, int x, int y) { super(id); this.x = x; this.y = y; }
    public void dispatch(UIComponent c) { c.handle(this); }
}

class KeyEvent extends BaseEvent {
    public final char key;
    public KeyEvent(int id, char k) { super(id); this.key = k; }
    public void dispatch(UIComponent c) { c.handle(this); }
}

// 2. THE COMPONENTS HIERARCHY
interface UIComponent {
    void onEvent(UIEvent e); // Entry point
    void handle(ClickEvent c);
    void handle(ScrollEvent s);
    void handle(DragEvent d);
    void handle(KeyEvent k);
}

abstract class BaseComponent implements UIComponent {
    // Default: Ignore unhandled events
    public void onEvent(UIEvent e) { e.dispatch(this); }
    public void handle(ClickEvent c) { /* Ignore */ }
    public void handle(ScrollEvent s) { /* Ignore */ }
    public void handle(DragEvent d) { /* Ignore */ }
    public void handle(KeyEvent k) { /* Ignore */ }
}

class Button extends BaseComponent {
    private String label;
    private Runnable action;
    
    public Button(String label, Runnable action) {
        this.label = label;
        this.action = action;
    }

    @Override
    public void handle(ClickEvent c) {
        System.out.println("🔘 Button '" + label + "' Clicked! Executing Action...");
        if (action != null) action.run();
    }
    
    // Buttons don't scroll or type, so defaults apply
}

class Window extends BaseComponent {
    private String title;
    private int scrollY = 0;
    
    public Window(String title) { this.title = title; }

    @Override
    public void handle(ClickEvent c) {
        System.out.println("🪟 Window '" + title + "' Focused (Brought to Front).");
    }

    @Override
    public void handle(ScrollEvent s) {
        this.scrollY += s.deltaY;
        System.out.println("🪟 Window '" + title + "' Scrolled to Y=" + scrollY);
    }
    
    @Override
    public void handle(DragEvent d) {
        System.out.println("🪟 Window '" + title + "' Dragged to " + d.x + "," + d.y);
    }
}

class TextField extends BaseComponent {
    private StringBuilder content = new StringBuilder();

    @Override
    public void handle(ClickEvent c) {
        System.out.println("📝 TextField Focused. Ready to type.");
    }
    
    @Override
    public void handle(KeyEvent k) {
        content.append(k.key);
        System.out.println("📝 Text: " + content.toString());
    }
}

// 3. EVENT BUS DISPATCHER
class EventBus {
    private List<UIComponent> subscribers = new ArrayList<>();
    
    public void subscribe(UIComponent c) { subscribers.add(c); }
    
    public void broadcast(UIEvent e) {
        System.out.println("📢 Broadcasting: " + e);
        for (UIComponent c : subscribers) {
            c.onEvent(e);
        }
    }
}
```

#### **Project 2: Universal Document Converter**
**Scenario**: Converting complex document structures (Paragraphs, Tables, Images) into different formats (HTML, Markdown, PlainText).
**Pattern**: Visitor (Double Dispatch).

```java
import java.util.*;

// 1. ELEMENTS
interface DocElement {
    void accept(DocVisitor v);
}

class Paragraph implements DocElement {
    String text;
    public Paragraph(String t) { this.text = t; }
    public void accept(DocVisitor v) { v.visit(this); }
}

class Image implements DocElement {
    String src;
    public Image(String s) { this.src = s; }
    public void accept(DocVisitor v) { v.visit(this); }
}

class Table implements DocElement {
    List<List<String>> data;
    public Table(List<List<String>> d) { this.data = d; }
    public void accept(DocVisitor v) { v.visit(this); }
}

class CodeBlock implements DocElement {
    String code;
    String lang;
    public CodeBlock(String c, String l) { this.code = c; this.lang = l; }
    public void accept(DocVisitor v) { v.visit(this); }
}

// 2. VISITORS (The Converters)
interface DocVisitor {
    void visit(Paragraph p);
    void visit(Image i);
    void visit(Table t);
    void visit(CodeBlock c);
}

class HtmlExporter implements DocVisitor {
    StringBuilder sb = new StringBuilder();
    public void visit(Paragraph p) { sb.append("<p>" + p.text + "</p>\n"); }
    public void visit(Image i) { sb.append("<img src='" + i.src + "'/>\n"); }
    public void visit(CodeBlock c) { 
        sb.append("<pre><code class='" + c.lang + "'>" + c.code + "</code></pre>\n"); 
    }
    public void visit(Table t) {
        sb.append("<table>\n");
        for (List<String> row : t.data) {
            sb.append("  <tr>");
            for (String cell : row) sb.append("<td>" + cell + "</td>");
            sb.append("</tr>\n");
        }
        sb.append("</table>\n");
    }
}

class MarkdownExporter implements DocVisitor {
    StringBuilder sb = new StringBuilder();
    public void visit(Paragraph p) { sb.append(p.text + "\n\n"); }
    public void visit(Image i) { sb.append("![](" + i.src + ")\n"); }
    public void visit(CodeBlock c) { 
        sb.append("```" + c.lang + "\n" + c.code + "\n```\n"); 
    }
    public void visit(Table t) {
        for (List<String> row : t.data) {
            sb.append("| " + String.join(" | ", row) + " |\n");
        }
    }
}
```

#### **Project 3: Cross-Border Payment Processor**
**Scenario**: Handling payments depends on **Region** (EU/US) AND **CardType** (Visa/Amex).
*   **EU + Visa**: Standard.
*   **EU + Amex**: High Fees.
*   **US + Visa**: Standard.

```java
// 1. REGIONS
interface Region {
    void processPayment(PaymentMethod pm, double amount);
    void processVisa(Visa v, double amount);
    void processAmex(Amex a, double amount);
    void processMastercard(Mastercard m, double amount);
    void processCrypto(Crypto c, double amount);
}

class Europe implements Region {
    public void processPayment(PaymentMethod pm, double amount) { pm.processIn(this, amount); }
    public void processVisa(Visa v, double amount) { System.out.println("🇪🇺 EU Visa: 1% Fee."); }
    public void processAmex(Amex a, double amount) { System.out.println("🇪🇺 EU Amex: 3% Fee (Surcharge)."); }
    public void processMastercard(Mastercard m, double amount) { System.out.println("🇪🇺 EU Mastercard: 1.2% Fee."); }
    public void processCrypto(Crypto c, double amount) { System.out.println("🇪🇺 EU Crypto: Regulatory Check Required."); }
}

class US implements Region {
    public void processPayment(PaymentMethod pm, double amount) { pm.processIn(this, amount); }
    public void processVisa(Visa v, double amount) { System.out.println("🇺🇸 US Visa: 1.5% Fee."); }
    public void processAmex(Amex a, double amount) { System.out.println("🇺🇸 US Amex: 2% Fee (Preferred)."); }

class APAC implements Region {

    public void processCrypto(Crypto c, double amount) { System.out.println("🌏 APAC Crypto: BANNED."); }
}

// 2. PAYMENT METHODS

}
class Visa implements PaymentMethod { public void processIn(Region r, double a) { r.processVisa(this, a); } }
class Amex implements PaymentMethod { public void processIn(Region r, double a) { r.processAmex(this, a); } }
class Mastercard implements PaymentMethod { public void processIn(Region r, double a) { r.processMastercard(this, a); } }
```

#### **Project 5: Compiler Type Checker**
**Scenario**: Validating operations in an AST.
*   `Integer` + `Integer` -> Valid.
*   `Integer` + `String` -> Error.
*   `Float` + `Integer` -> Promote to Float.

```java
interface Type {
    Type add(Type other);
    Type addInteger(IntegerType i);
    Type addFloat(FloatType f);
    Type addString(StringType s);
}

class IntegerType implements Type {
    public Type add(Type other) { return other.addInteger(this); }
    
    public Type addInteger(IntegerType i) { return this; } // Int + Int = Int
    public Type addFloat(FloatType f) { return f; }        // Int + Float = Float
    public Type addString(StringType s) { throw new RuntimeException("Type Error"); }
}

class FloatType implements Type {
    public Type add(Type other) { return other.addFloat(this); }
    
    public Type addInteger(IntegerType i) { return this; } // Float + Int = Float
    public Type addFloat(FloatType f) { return this; }     // Float + Float = Float
    public Type addString(StringType s) { throw new RuntimeException("Type Error"); }
}
```

#### **Project 6: AST Optimizer (Constant Folding)**
**Scenario**: You have an AST (Abstract Syntax Tree) for a math expression. You want to optimize `Add(Lit(1), Lit(2))` into `Lit(3)` at compile time.
**Pattern**: Visitor with modification (returning a new Node).

```java
// 1. AST Definition (Same as Deep Dive but expanded)
interface Node {
    <R> R accept(NodeVisitor<R> visitor);
}

class Literal implements Node {
    final int value;
    Literal(int v) { this.value = v; }
    public <R> R accept(NodeVisitor<R> v) { return v.visit(this); }
    public String toString() { return String.valueOf(value); }
}

class BinaryOp implements Node {
    final String op;
    final Node left, right;
    BinaryOp(String op, Node l, Node r) { this.op = op; this.left = l; this.right = r; }
    public <R> R accept(NodeVisitor<R> v) { return v.visit(this); }
    public String toString() { return "(" + left + " " + op + " " + right + ")"; }
}

// 2. VISITOR INTERFACE
interface NodeVisitor<R> {
    R visit(Literal n);
    R visit(BinaryOp n);
}

// 3. OPTIMIZER VISITOR (Reduces the tree)
class Optimizer implements NodeVisitor<Node> {
    
    public Node visit(Literal n) {
        return n; // Literals are already optimal
    }
    
    public Node visit(BinaryOp n) {
        // First, optimize children (Post-Order Traversal)
        Node optLeft = n.left.accept(this);
        Node optRight = n.right.accept(this);
        
        // If both children are Literals, we can fold them!
        if (optLeft instanceof Literal && optRight instanceof Literal) {
            int lVal = ((Literal) optLeft).value;
            int rVal = ((Literal) optRight).value;
            
            if (n.op.equals("+")) return new Literal(lVal + rVal);
            if (n.op.equals("-")) return new Literal(lVal - rVal);
            if (n.op.equals("*")) return new Literal(lVal * rVal);
        }
        
        // If no optimization possible, return a new Node with optimized children
        return new BinaryOp(n.op, optLeft, optRight);
    }
}

// 4. USAGE
public class OptimizerDemo {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        // Tree: (5 + 3) * (2 + 0)
        Node root = new BinaryOp("*",
            new BinaryOp("+", new Literal(5), new Literal(3)),
            new BinaryOp("+", new Literal(2), new Literal(0))
        );
        
        System.out.println("Original: " + root);
        
        Optimizer opt = new Optimizer();
        Node optimized = root.accept(opt);
        
        System.out.println("Optimized: " + optimized); // should be "16"
    }
}
```

#### **Project 7: Financial Audit System**
**Scenario**: A bank has multiple Asset types (Stocks, Bonds, RealEstate, Cash). An auditor needs to calculate Total Value, Risk Exposure, and Tax Liability.
**Pattern**: Multiple Visitors for different business reports.

```java
import java.util.*;

// 1. ASSETS
interface Asset {
    <T> T accept(AssetVisitor<T> visitor);
}

class Stock implements Asset {
    String ticker;
    double price;
    int quantity;
    double volatility; // 0.0 to 1.0
    
    public Stock(String t, double p, int q, double v) {
        this.ticker = t; this.price = p; this.quantity = q; this.volatility = v;
    }
    public <T> T accept(AssetVisitor<T> v) { return v.visit(this); }
}

class RealEstate implements Asset {
    double estimatedValue;
    boolean isRental;
    
    public RealEstate(double v, boolean r) { this.estimatedValue = v; this.isRental = r; }
    public <T> T accept(AssetVisitor<T> v) { return v.visit(this); }
}

class Bond implements Asset {
    double principal;
    double rate;
    int yearsRemaining;
    
    public Bond(double p, double r, int y) { this.principal = p; this.rate = r; this.yearsRemaining = y; }
    public <T> T accept(AssetVisitor<T> v) { return v.visit(this); }
}

// 2. VISITOR INTERFACE
interface AssetVisitor<T> {
    T visit(Stock s);
    T visit(RealEstate r);
    T visit(Bond b);
}

// 3. NET WORTH VISITOR (Returns Double)
class NetWorthVisitor implements AssetVisitor<Double> {
    public Double visit(Stock s) { return s.price * s.quantity; }
    public Double visit(RealEstate r) { return r.estimatedValue; }
    public Double visit(Bond b) { return b.principal; } // Simplified
}

// 4. TAX VISITOR (Returns Double)
class TaxLiabilityVisitor implements AssetVisitor<Double> {
    public Double visit(Stock s) {
        // 15% Capital Gains on arbitrary 10% gain assumption
        return (s.price * s.quantity) * 0.10 * 0.15; 
    }
    public Double visit(RealEstate r) {
        // 1.2% Property Tax
        return r.estimatedValue * 0.012;
    }
    public Double visit(Bond b) {
        // Interest is taxed as income
        return (b.principal * b.rate) * 0.30;
    }
}

// 5. RISK ANALYSIS VISITOR (Returns String Report)
class RiskReportVisitor implements AssetVisitor<String> {
    public String visit(Stock s) {
        if (s.volatility > 0.8) return "High Risk Stock: " + s.ticker;
        return "Stable Stock: " + s.ticker;
    }
    public String visit(RealEstate r) {
        if (r.estimatedValue > 1_000_000) return "Concentrated Asset: Real Estate";
        return "Safe Real Estate";
    }
    public String visit(Bond b) {
        if (b.yearsRemaining > 10) return "Long-term Bond Risk";
        return "Safe Bond";
    }
}

// usage example...
```

#### **Project 8: DevOps Pipeline Validator**
**Scenario**: A CI/CD pipeline is defined as a tree of Steps. Validate that:
1.  No step uses `sudo`.
2.  All `Deploy` steps have a `ManualApproval` predecessor.
3.  Timeout is set for every script.

```java
import java.util.*;

// 1. PIPELINE ELEMENTS
interface PipelineStep {
    void accept(PipelineVisitor v);
}

class BuildStage implements PipelineStep {
    String image;
    boolean usesSudo;
    public BuildStage(String i, boolean s) { this.image = i; this.usesSudo = s; }
    public void accept(PipelineVisitor v) { v.visit(this); }
}

class DeployStage implements PipelineStep {
    String targetEnv;
    boolean manualWait;
    public DeployStage(String t, boolean m) { this.targetEnv = t; this.manualWait = m; }
    public void accept(PipelineVisitor v) { v.visit(this); }
}

class TestStage implements PipelineStep {
    int timeoutSeconds;
    public TestStage(int t) { this.timeoutSeconds = t; }
    public void accept(PipelineVisitor v) { v.visit(this); }
}

class ScriptStep implements PipelineStep {
    String commands;
    public ScriptStep(String c) { this.commands = c; }
    public void accept(PipelineVisitor v) { v.visit(this); }
}

// 2. VISITOR INTERFACE
interface PipelineVisitor {
    void visit(BuildStage s);
    void visit(DeployStage s);
    void visit(TestStage s);
    void visit(ScriptStep s);
}

// 3. SECURITY VALIDATOR VISITOR
class SecurityValidator implements PipelineVisitor {
    List<String> violations = new ArrayList<>();
    
    public void visit(BuildStage s) {
        if (s.usesSudo) violations.add("CRITICAL: Root access ('sudo') detected in Build.");
        if (!s.image.startsWith("company-repo/")) violations.add("WARNING: Using public Docker image: " + s.image);
    }
    
    public void visit(DeployStage s) {
        if (s.targetEnv.equals("PROD") && !s.manualWait) {
            violations.add("CRITICAL: PROD deployment requires manual approval step.");
        }
    }
    
    public void visit(TestStage s) { /* Safe */ }
    
    public void visit(ScriptStep s) {
        if (s.commands.contains("curl")) violations.add("WARNING: Fetching external scripts via curl.");
        if (s.commands.contains("rm -rf /")) violations.add("CRITICAL: Destructive command detected.");
    }
}

// 4. EXECUTION PLANNER VISITOR
class ExecutionTimeEstimator implements PipelineVisitor {
    int totalSeconds = 0;
    
    public void visit(BuildStage s) { totalSeconds += 300; } // Avg 5 mins
    public void visit(DeployStage s) { totalSeconds += 60; }
    public void visit(TestStage s) { totalSeconds += s.timeoutSeconds; }
    public void visit(ScriptStep s) { totalSeconds += 10; }
}

// 5. USAGE
public class DevOpsDemo {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        List<PipelineStep> pipeline = List.of(
            new BuildStage("ubuntu:latest", true), // Unsafe!
            new TestStage(120),
            new DeployStage("PROD", false)         // Unsafe!
        );
        
        SecurityValidator scanner = new SecurityValidator();
        for (PipelineStep step : pipeline) step.accept(scanner);
        
        if (!scanner.violations.isEmpty()) {
            System.out.println("❌ Pipeline Rejected:");
            scanner.violations.forEach(System.out::println);
        } else {
            System.out.println("✅ Pipeline Approved.");
        }
    }
}
```

```java
// 1. CARGO & ROUTES (Double Dispatch on both?)
// Standard Visitor only dispatches on Element (Cargo). 
// Here we have Cargo types (Hazardous, Normal) and Route types (Road, Air).

interface Cargo {
    void transport(Route r);
}

class RegularCargo implements Cargo {
    public void transport(Route r) { r.handleRegular(this); }
}

class HazardousCargo implements Cargo {
    public void transport(Route r) { r.handleHazardous(this); }
}

class PerishableCargo implements Cargo {
    public void transport(Route r) { r.handlePerishable(this); }
}

// 2. ROUTE VISITOR
interface Route {
    void handleRegular(RegularCargo c);
    void handleHazardous(HazardousCargo c);
    void handlePerishable(PerishableCargo c);
}

// 3. IMPLEMENTATIONS
class TruckRoute implements Route {
    public void handleRegular(RegularCargo c) { System.out.println("🚛 Truck: Normal shipping. $100"); }
    public void handleHazardous(HazardousCargo c) { System.out.println("🚛 Truck: Hazmat license required. $500"); }
    public void handlePerishable(PerishableCargo c) { System.out.println("🚛 Truck: Refrigerated trailer. $300"); }
}

class AirRoute implements Route {
    public void handleRegular(RegularCargo c) { System.out.println("✈️ Air: Express shipping. $1000"); }
    public void handleHazardous(HazardousCargo c) { System.out.println("✈️ Air: REJECTED. Cannot fly hazmat."); }
    public void handlePerishable(PerishableCargo c) { System.out.println("✈️ Air: Fast delivery (Fresh). $1200"); }
}

class ShipRoute implements Route {
    public void handleRegular(RegularCargo c) { System.out.println("🚢 Ship: Slow shipping. $20"); }
    public void handleHazardous(HazardousCargo c) { System.out.println("🚢 Ship: Container locked. $100"); }
    public void handlePerishable(PerishableCargo c) { System.out.println("🚢 Ship: REJECTED. Too slow."); }
}

// 4. USAGE
public class LogisticsDemo {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        List<Cargo> manifest = List.of(new HazardousCargo(), new PerishableCargo());
        Route air = new AirRoute();
        
        System.out.println("--- Air Freight Manifest ---");

            item.transport(air);
        }
    }
}
```

#### **Project 11: Game AI Behavior Tree**
**Scenario**: You are building an NPC AI logic using Behavior Trees. The tree structure describes *logic* (Sequence, Selector, Decorator), while the execution is handled by a Visitor.
**Pattern**: Stateful Visitor (maintaining execution context).

```java
import java.util.*;

// 1. BEHAVIOR NODES
interface BehaviorNode {
    NodeStatus accept(BehaviorVisitor v);
}

enum NodeStatus { SUCCESS, FAILURE, RUNNING }

class SequenceNode implements BehaviorNode {
    List<BehaviorNode> children = new ArrayList<>();
    public SequenceNode(BehaviorNode... nodes) { Collections.addAll(children, nodes); }
    public NodeStatus accept(BehaviorVisitor v) { return v.visit(this); }
}

class SelectorNode implements BehaviorNode {
    List<BehaviorNode> children = new ArrayList<>();
    public SelectorNode(BehaviorNode... nodes) { Collections.addAll(children, nodes); }
    public NodeStatus accept(BehaviorVisitor v) { return v.visit(this); }
}

class ActionNode implements BehaviorNode {
    String name;
    public ActionNode(String n) { this.name = n; }
    public NodeStatus accept(BehaviorVisitor v) { return v.visit(this); }
}

class ConditionNode implements BehaviorNode {
    String condition;
    public ConditionNode(String c) { this.condition = c; }
    public NodeStatus accept(BehaviorVisitor v) { return v.visit(this); }
}

class InverterNode implements BehaviorNode {
    BehaviorNode child;
    public InverterNode(BehaviorNode c) { this.child = c; }
    public NodeStatus accept(BehaviorVisitor v) { return v.visit(this); }
}

// 2. VISITOR INTERFACE
interface BehaviorVisitor {
    NodeStatus visit(SequenceNode n);
    NodeStatus visit(SelectorNode n);
    NodeStatus visit(ActionNode n);
    NodeStatus visit(ConditionNode n);
    NodeStatus visit(InverterNode n);
}

// 3. EXECUTION VISITOR
class ExecutionVisitor implements BehaviorVisitor {
    // Simulated Blackboard (World State)
    Map<String, Boolean> worldState = new HashMap<>();
    
    public ExecutionVisitor() {
        // Initial State
        worldState.put("EnemyVisible", true);
        worldState.put("HasAmmo", false);
        worldState.put("HasCover", true);
    }

    public NodeStatus visit(SequenceNode n) {
        System.out.println("-> Sequence");
        for (BehaviorNode child : n.children) {
            NodeStatus status = child.accept(this);
            if (status == NodeStatus.FAILURE) return NodeStatus.FAILURE;
            if (status == NodeStatus.RUNNING) return NodeStatus.RUNNING;
        }
        return NodeStatus.SUCCESS;
    }

    public NodeStatus visit(SelectorNode n) {
        System.out.println("-> Selector");
        for (BehaviorNode child : n.children) {
            NodeStatus status = child.accept(this);
            if (status == NodeStatus.SUCCESS) return NodeStatus.SUCCESS;
            if (status == NodeStatus.RUNNING) return NodeStatus.RUNNING;
        }
        return NodeStatus.FAILURE;
    }

    public NodeStatus visit(ActionNode n) {
        System.out.println("   [Action] " + n.name);
        // Simulate logic
        if (n.name.equals("Reload") && !worldState.get("HasAmmo")) {
            worldState.put("HasAmmo", true);
            return NodeStatus.SUCCESS;
        }
        return NodeStatus.SUCCESS; 
    }

    public NodeStatus visit(ConditionNode n) {
        boolean result = worldState.getOrDefault(n.condition, false);
        System.out.println("   [Condition] " + n.condition + "? " + result);
        return result ? NodeStatus.SUCCESS : NodeStatus.FAILURE;
    }
    
    public NodeStatus visit(InverterNode n) {
        System.out.println("-> Inverter");
        NodeStatus status = n.child.accept(this);
        if (status == NodeStatus.SUCCESS) return NodeStatus.FAILURE;
        if (status == NodeStatus.FAILURE) return NodeStatus.SUCCESS;
        return status;
    }
}

// 4. USAGE
public class AiDemo {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        // AI Logic: IF (EnemyVisible) THEN (AttackSequence) ELSE (Patrol)
        // AttackSequence: IF (HasAmmo) THEN (Shoot) ELSE (Reload)
        
        BehaviorNode attackLogic = new SelectorNode(
            new SequenceNode(
                new ConditionNode("HasAmmo"),
                new ActionNode("Shoot")
            ),
            new ActionNode("Reload")
        );
        
        BehaviorNode root = new SelectorNode(
            new SequenceNode(
                new ConditionNode("EnemyVisible"),
                attackLogic
            ),
            new ActionNode("Patrol")
        );
        
        ExecutionVisitor engine = new ExecutionVisitor();
        System.out.println("--- AI Update Tick 1 ---");
        root.accept(engine);
    }
}
```

#### **Project 12: SQL Query Generator (Type-Safe Builder)**
**Scenario**: Build a type-safe SQL query API (like JOOQ or Hibernate Criteria) that generates SQL strings by visiting an AST of clauses.
**Pattern**: Visitor for recursive string generation.

```java
import java.util.*;

// 1. QUERY AST NODES
interface QueryPart {
    void accept(SqlVisitor v);
}

class Select implements QueryPart {
    List<String> columns;
    public Select(String... cols) { this.columns = Arrays.asList(cols); }
    public void accept(SqlVisitor v) { v.visit(this); }
}

class From implements QueryPart {
    String table;
    public From(String t) { this.table = t; }
    public void accept(SqlVisitor v) { v.visit(this); }
}

class Where implements QueryPart {
    String condition;
    public Where(String c) { this.condition = c; }
    public void accept(SqlVisitor v) { v.visit(this); }
}

class Join implements QueryPart {
    String table;
    String on;
    public Join(String t, String on) { this.table = t; this.on = on; }
    public void accept(SqlVisitor v) { v.visit(this); }
}

class FullQuery implements QueryPart {
    Select select;
    From from;
    List<Join> joins = new ArrayList<>();
    Where where;
    
    public FullQuery(Select s, From f) { this.select = s; this.from = f; }
    public void addJoin(Join j) { joins.add(j); }
    public void setWhere(Where w) { this.where = w; }
    
    public void accept(SqlVisitor v) { v.visit(this); }
}

// 2. VISITOR
interface SqlVisitor {
    void visit(Select s);
    void visit(From f);
    void visit(Where w);
    void visit(Join j);
    void visit(FullQuery q);
}

// 3. POSTGRE-SQL GENERATOR
class PostgresGenerator implements SqlVisitor {
    StringBuilder sb = new StringBuilder();
    
    public String getSql() { return sb.toString(); }
    
    public void visit(FullQuery q) {
        q.select.accept(this);
        q.from.accept(this);
        for (Join j : q.joins) j.accept(this);
        if (q.where != null) q.where.accept(this);
        sb.append(";");
    }
    
    public void visit(Select s) {
        sb.append("SELECT ");
        sb.append(String.join(", ", s.columns));
    }
    
    public void visit(From f) {
        sb.append("\nFROM ").append(f.table);
    }
    
    public void visit(Join j) {
        sb.append("\nJOIN ").append(j.table).append(" ON ").append(j.on);
    }
    
    public void visit(Where w) {
        sb.append("\nWHERE ").append(w.condition);
    }
}

// 4. USAGE
public class SqlDemo {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        // SELECT id, name FROM users JOIN orders ON users.id = orders.uid WHERE active = true
        FullQuery query = new FullQuery(
            new Select("id", "name", "email"),
            new From("users")
        );
        query.addJoin(new Join("orders", "users.id = orders.user_id"));
        query.setWhere(new Where("users.active = true AND orders.total > 100"));
        
        PostgresGenerator pg = new PostgresGenerator();
        query.accept(pg);
        
        System.out.println(pg.getSql());
    }
}
```
